title: fix(deps): take the patched h2, and document the line that has no patch
body:
## The advisory

**RUSTSEC-2026-0258** — h2 accepts and queues empty DATA frames without limit.
A peer that never drains can drive unbounded memory growth, or a panic if the
length overflows. Upstream rates it **Low** and patched it in **0.4.16**.

The graph carried two h2 lines. They end differently, and the difference is the
whole PR.

## 0.4.14 → 0.4.16 — fixed

A straight bump to the patched release.

The lockfile moves **exactly one package**. I checked this rather than eyeball
the diff, because the raw diff also shows `windows-sys`, `syn` and `socket2`
lines that look like downgrades — they are dependency-list ordering inside
packages that already had both versions in the graph:

```
REMOVED: ['h2@0.4.14']
ADDED:   ['h2@0.4.16']
```

## 0.3.27 — cannot be fixed here, now an explicit exception

There is no version to move to: **0.3.27 is the newest 0.3**, and upstream
patched only the 0.4 line.

It arrives as `hyper 0.14 → hyper-tls 0.5 → reqwest 0.11 → ssi-dids-core 0.1.3
→ affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk`, reaching **`trust-tasks-tsp`** (via
`affinidi-tsp`) and **`trust-tasks-proof`**. That is the *normal* graph, not a
dev-dependency — crates we publish link it.

Nothing in this repo can shorten that chain:

- our requirements are already open — `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk = "0.8"`,
  `affinidi-tsp = "0.1"`
- every 0.8.x of the resolver SDK **up to and including the newest, 0.8.22**,
  requires `ssi-dids-core ^0.1`
- `ssi-dids-core 0.1` is what pins reqwest 0.11, hence hyper 0.14, hence h2 0.3

I tried bumping the Affinidi crates (0.8.7 → 0.8.13, affinidi-tsp 0.1.6 →
0.1.14). It does not clear the advisory and churns the lockfile substantially,
so it is deliberately **not** in this PR.

### Exposure, stated rather than waved away

`reqwest` is an HTTP **client** here, used to resolve DIDs. Reaching the flaw
needs a hostile or compromised resolution endpoint, and the cost is
availability only — memory growth or a panic, with no confidentiality or
integrity component. That is the entire argument for accepting it, and it is an
argument for accepting it *temporarily*.

### Why this exception is different from the others

Every entry already in `deny.toml`'s ignore list is a **maintenance-status**
notice that says "no active CVE". This is the first that is a real
vulnerability. The comment marks it as such so nobody reads the list as
uniformly harmless, and states the clearing condition: it goes when
`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` moves to `ssi-dids-core 0.3+`, which is on
reqwest 0.12 / hyper 1.x and so on the patched h2 line. Worth re-checking
whenever the Affinidi crates are bumped.

## Why this is a separate PR

It surfaced on #240, but that PR only adds JSON Schemas and touches neither
`Cargo.lock` nor `Cargo.toml`. The advisory was published after main's last
green run, so **main fails it too** — this is not a regression from #240 and
should not be buried in a spec change.

## Test

- `cargo deny check` — clean across advisories, bans, licenses, sources
- `cargo test --workspace` — **493 passing, 0 failures**

title: chore(ts): declare the bindings side-effect free
body:
## What

Adds `"sideEffects": false` to `trust-tasks-ts/package.json`.

## Why

Every generated module is a pure `export const` / `export type` — there is no
module-level work anywhere in the package. Without this flag a bundler has to
assume otherwise and keeps every task family a consumer touches, because it
cannot prove that dropping one is safe.

The bindings are large and growing (328 modules at present) and consumers
typically import a handful of families. `@openvtc/pnm-core` is the immediate
beneficiary: it is heading for a browser extension bundle, where the MV3
service worker is a single Rollup output with no code splitting, so anything
tree-shaking cannot remove is carried at runtime.

## Risk

The claim is checkable and true today: the flag is a lie only if a module gains
an import with a side effect or does work at module scope. Nothing in the
generator emits either — it writes constants and types.

## Test

No behaviour to test; `npm run build` in `trust-tasks-ts` is unchanged.
author: stormer78

title: chore(ts): declare the bindings side-effect free (#239)
body:
chore(ts): declare the bindings side-effect free (#239)

Every generated module is data — payload interfaces, TYPE_URI / SPEC
constants — and the hand-written _runtime pipeline initialises nothing beyond
its own module-scoped Set and RegExp. Nothing here patches a global, so
importing a module a consumer never uses is safe to drop.

Without the declaration a bundler has to keep all of it. That matters for the
browser consumers this package is aimed at: a web console that imports one
task family should not ship the schema constants of the other 269. Verified
against the existing build and test suite.

title: feat(didcomm-v1-crate): implement binding 0.2 — the dedicated type, the omit rule, receivers move first (#238)
body:
feat(didcomm-v1-crate): implement binding 0.2 — the dedicated type, the omit rule, receivers move first (#238)

The reference crate lagged the specification it implements, on both rules
the binding gained since 0.1:

The carriage (0.2 §2): build_message now emits the binding's own message
type — the RFC 0020 URI …/trust-task/1.0/task — with the document in the
reserved ~attach entry and the advisory human-readable line moved from
basic-message's content to the dedicated type's comment member. Per §2.3
receivers move first: unpack_trust_task accepts BOTH carriages, the
dedicated type and 0.1's basic-message, while the producer emits only the
former.

The omit rule (§4, from #208): ~thread values must satisfy RFC 0008's
shape. A threadId, parentThreadId, or fallback id that cannot be
represented — urn:uuid: ids most prominently — is omitted, never
rewritten: a rewritten correlator contradicts the in-band member and
draws a guaranteed malformedRequest from the consumer's comparison. The
consumer side already read explicit_thid(), so a defaulted thid was
never treated as an assertion; the module docs now say why.

Version to 0.8.0 — producer output changes type, which is a behavioural
break for any consumer gating on basic-message. Tests 11 → 13: the omit
rule (member, fallback, and boundary cases), the dedicated-type shape,
the comment member, and the §2.3 legacy-acceptance gate.

Signed-off-by: Alberto L <aleon@law.harvard.edu>
author: albertoleon7794

title: feat(didcomm-v1-crate): implement binding 0.2 — dedicated type, omit rule, receivers move first
body:
The reference crate still implemented the binding as it stood at 0.1; the specification moved twice and this closes the gap — the follow-up offered in #173 ("still yours, as offered") after #208 and #216.

**The carriage (0.2 §2).** `build_message` now emits the binding's dedicated message type (`…/binding/didcomm-v1/0.2/trust-task/1.0/task`) with the document in the reserved `trust-task` attachment, and the advisory human-readable line moved from basic-message's `content` to the dedicated type's `comment`. Per §2.3 — receivers move first — `unpack_trust_task` accepts **both** carriages (the dedicated type and 0.1's basic-message) while the producer emits only the new one.

**The omit rule (§4, from #208).** `~thread` values must satisfy RFC 0008's shape; a `threadId`, `parentThreadId`, or fallback `id` that cannot be represented (`urn:uuid:` ids most prominently) is **omitted, never rewritten** — a rewritten correlator contradicts the in-band member and draws a guaranteed `malformedRequest` from the consumer's §3.1 comparison. The consumer side already compared `explicit_thid()` only, so a defaulted `thid` was never treated as an assertion; the docs now state that rule rather than leaving it implicit.

Version 0.7.0 → **0.8.0**: the producer's output changes message type, a behavioural break for any consumer gating on basic-message (per the workspace's semver-over-the-library rule). Tests 11 → 13 — the omit rule (member, fallback, boundaries), the dedicated-type shape, the `comment` member, and the §2.3 legacy-acceptance gate. `cargo test` / `clippy -D warnings` / `fmt` clean.

Validated against the deployed consumer side: the same carriage shape (type + `trust-task` attachment + omit rule) is what Credo 0.6.3 agents have been exercising in the Keyring reference ladder — [ref-06v1c](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06v1c-task-layer) runs it live including the §2.3 legacy check, and [ref-06x](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06x-cypress-stack) end-to-end at the Cypress release.

**TL;DR: the reference crate now implements binding 0.2 as published — dedicated `@type` out, both carriages in (receivers move first), and the #208 omit rule for unrepresentable thread ids. 0.8.0, 13 tests, clippy/fmt clean.**

title: fix(logs): name the speaking identity in a listener's profile label
body:
## Problem

The messaging-profile label named the community and nothing else:

```rust
let Some(c) = membership else { return "Persona".to_string() };
c.display_name.clone()
    .or_else(|| agent_name(&c.vtc_did))     // the COMMUNITY's name
    .unwrap_or_else(|| c.vtc_did.clone())
```

That is many-to-one over listeners in three separate ways, all observed in live debug logs:

* **Two personas in the same community produced byte-identical labels.** From a local run: two different DIDs (`QmRpzDL…`, `Qmb1FSz…`) both logging as `profile=webvh.storm.ws/@first-vtc`.
* **A persona in several communities** took whichever membership `find` happened to return first, so the label was not even stable across runs.
* **A persona with no community was labelled the literal string `"Persona"`** — which every State-A listener therefore shared. That is what a remote user's log showed.

This label names the messaging profile, so it is what the transport stamps on every `websocket_run{profile=…}` span, and what a mediator-side log has to be correlated against. Reading one of those logs, a single listener reconnecting and several listeners reconnecting on their own schedules are indistinguishable — which is exactly the confusion that made a reconnect investigation take two capture rounds to resolve. I misread a correct log as a regression because of it.

Same defect the activity log had (#231), one layer down and worse placed: the transport log is where you drop to *when the activity log is not enough*.

## Fix

Each label now carries the persona's own DID beside the community, truncated at the same width the R-DID labels already use for their remote DID so the two read alike:

```
Acme Corp (did:webvh:QmScidPersonaAAAAAA...)
Persona (did:webvh:QmScidPersonaAAAAAA...)      ← no community yet
```

`membership_profile_label` takes the persona DID as a parameter rather than reaching for it, because its two callers hold it differently: the runtime resolves it from `Config::identities`, while the loading path has it in hand before any `Config` exists.

**Display-only.** `ListenerSpec::label` feeds the profile name and `Debug`; nothing matches on it. This changes what logs say, not what the transport does.

## Tests

Two personas in one community are distinguishable; the no-community case carries its DID; a DID short enough not to need truncating is carried whole; plus the existing precedence cases (display name > verified agent name > VTC DID) updated for the new shape.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` — all green.

title: chore(deps): take the TDK auth fix (tdk-common 0.6.8, did-auth 0.3.11)
body:
Picks up [affinidi-tdk-rs#716](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/716), which stops a proactive token refresh from silently doing nothing.

## What it fixes

The websocket transport refreshes at 80% of the access token's life and rebuilds the socket to carry the new token. The refresh was a no-op — the `force_refresh` intent was dropped before the code that acts on it — so each rebuild re-armed the deadline at 80% of the time *remaining*. On a 900 s token, per profile:

```
T-180s   teardown + reconnect, token unchanged
T-36s    teardown + reconnect, token unchanged
T-7s     teardown + reconnect, token unchanged
expired  teardown + reconnect, token finally refreshed
```

Four teardowns per token per profile instead of one, the last two close enough together to trip our own `cycling rapidly` warning. That is the churn behind the "listeners keep connecting and disconnecting" reports — captured from a live mediator in two separate hour-long debug logs.

## Scope

Lockfile only, and only those two crates. **No manifest change is needed:** `affinidi-messaging-sdk` requires `affinidi-tdk-common = "0.6"`, and that caret already admits 0.6.8, which in turn pins `affinidi-did-authentication` 0.3.11.

The entries are edited in place rather than re-resolved. `cargo update -p affinidi-tdk-common` produces the same two upgrades *plus* 15 unrelated lines — 13 `windows-sys` references, `syn` and `base64` re-selected while the lockfile is rewritten — none of which this bump requires. `cargo metadata` accepts the edited file without rewriting it, so this is what cargo itself would resolve.

## Why the lockfile is the delivery mechanism

We commit `Cargo.lock`, so until this lands, anyone who pulls and rebuilds gets the old auth crates **however recently they ran `cargo update`** — cargo honours the lock. This is exactly what bit a user testing the fix: crates.io had 0.3.11/0.6.8 four hours before their run, they updated and rebuilt, and the flapping was unchanged.

To check any binary directly, without reasoning about lockfiles or which build got launched:

```bash
strings <openvtc-binary> | grep -c "still valid, but a refresh was requested"
```

`1` means the fix is compiled in; `0` means it is not. That string exists only in did-auth 0.3.11.

## Gate

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; `cargo deny check` — all green.

two close enough together to trip the `cycling rapidly` warning in our
own activity log. That is the reconnect churn behind the "listeners keep
connecting and disconnecting" reports.

Lockfile only, and only those two crates. No manifest change is needed:
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` requires `affinidi-tdk-common = "0.6"`, and the
caret already admits 0.6.8, which in turn pins did-auth 0.3.11.

The entries are edited in place rather than re-resolved. `cargo update`
produces the same two upgrades plus 15 unrelated lines — 13 `windows-sys`
references, `syn` and `base64` re-selected while the lockfile is
rewritten — none of which this bump requires. `cargo metadata` accepts
the edited file without rewriting it.

Why the lockfile matters here: we commit it, so until this lands anyone
who pulls and rebuilds still gets the old auth crates however recently
they ran `cargo update`. A binary that has the fix contains the string
"still valid, but a refresh was requested"; one that does not, does not.

Gate: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings; cargo test
--workspace; cargo deny check — all green.

title: fix(startup): bring listeners up off the loop, so Enter is not ignored
body:
## Problem

The loading screen offers "Press Enter to continue" once phase 1 finishes, and then ignores the keypress for seconds.

`state.loading_complete = true` is broadcast at `state_handler/mod.rs:712`. The runtime `select!` loop — the only thing that can service `Action::DismissLoading` — did not start until ~130 lines later. In between, that same thread awaited:

```rust
didcomm::install_listeners(&didcomm_service, &config, &tdk).await;
```

which walks the account's identities and, for each one, runs a mediator authentication handshake and a websocket connect — **in series**:

```rust
for spec in build_listener_configs(config, tdk).await {
    if service.has_listener(&spec.id).await { continue }
    add_listener(service, &spec).await          // auth + websocket
}
```

Nothing polls the action channel during that window, so the Enter was not lost — it queued, and the main page arrived in one late jump when the loop finally started. That reads as a freeze, and it grows with every identity on the account.

## Fix

The listener *specs* are still built on this thread, because that needs `Config`, which is not `Clone` and cannot cross into a task. Bringing the listeners **up** — the expensive half — now runs in a spawned task.

That is what the comment twenty lines below it already claimed:

> Phase 2 (community/persona DIDComm connection) runs ASYNCHRONOUSLY: we do NOT block the UI waiting for the listener.

The intent was documented; the implementation just didn't honour it.

## Why nothing downstream needs the sockets first

- A service with no listeners is already a supported state — `start_empty_service` exists for exactly that, and is what starts the runtime here.
- The session manager registers by listener id, not by a live socket.
- The runtime loop flips the connection status from typed lifecycle events as each listener lands, so the UI still reports Connecting → Connected correctly.
- The "registered listener" diagnostics move into the task, since what actually came up is only known once the installs finish.

`install_listeners` keeps its signature for its other caller and delegates to `connect_listeners`, the half that takes owned specs.

## Tests

Spawning the install returns immediately and has not installed the listener synchronously — driven with a spec whose mediator cannot resolve, so the install is demonstrably still in flight when the assertion runs.

The runtime loop itself is not factored into a test-callable unit (same limitation noted on #230), so the call-site ordering is not directly covered; the test pins the property of the function it now calls.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` — all green.

title: Trust Task Context Binding on published mechanisms, taskContext re-anchoring, and W3C proof/digest alignment
body:
Consolidated Working Draft 01 batch from the task force's working fork, superseding #15 by carrying it: the first commits are @bmiller59's #15 restructuring (authorship preserved), with three further changes built on top of it and the #15 first-pass review addressed. Closes #11. Resolves #17.

## What's inside, in order

**1. The #15 restructuring** (@bmiller59) — Trust Task Context Binding depends only on mechanisms already defined in the Trust Tasks core specification; the "qualifying specification" profile; outcome evidence travels with the presentation.

**2. `taskContext` re-anchoring and framework-0.4 alignment** — the outcome of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#173: `taskContext` carries the **`id` of the originating exchange's initiating document** (globally unique per the core specification's §4.3; the innermost exchange that attests the event, per §4.9.1), retiring the issuer-side uniqueness workaround. The qualifying profile is reworded against framework 0.4 (per-variant proof; the error variant honestly excluded — a task specification cannot strengthen `trust-task-error`'s own declaration; the no-`#response` escape hatch dropped). Outcome Interpretability cites the core specification's reply-disposition classification (§8.6) rather than hand-rolling the terminal/non-terminal split, and states the verifier's pairing checklist for retained evidence. A `trust-task-error` is failure evidence only, attributable to third parties when it carries `inResponseTo` (§8.2).

**3. W3C proof and digest alignment** (#17, all three items) — the VWC digest becomes `digestMultibase` (multibase multihash over the JCS canonical form the definition already named); multibase headers restricted to `z`/`u` per CID 1.0 §2.4 with alphabets enforced; proofs move from `Ed25519Signature2020` to the `DataIntegrityProof` envelope with `eddsa-jcs-2022` as the RECOMMENDED default suite (offline-verifiable; one canonicalization shared with `digestMultibase`) and `bbs-2023` named as the selective-disclosure path.

**4. The #15 first-pass review, addressed** — normative citations are commit-pinned permalinks (framework 0.4, `fbe196a`) so "pinned" is literally true; the stray subsection marking is removed; the per-issuer-uniqueness comment is mooted by the re-anchoring; and the term **"Trust Tasks core specification"** is now defined (`spec/terms-definitions/`), stating the core-vs-individual-specification architecture, explaining the upstream document's own "framework 0.4" version labels, and explicitly disclaiming the ToIP governance-framework sense.

## Evidence

The pairing checklist and the anchoring rule are executable: [`tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange) runs the witnessed exchange end-to-end — the VWC's `taskContext` lands on the ceremony's initiating document `id` structurally, and the retained `submit#response` passes exactly the checks the text states. The digest change is encoding-only for implementations already canonicalizing with JCS (verified against the Keyring witness implementation's own digest function).

Spec-Up-T render verified locally: every `[[ref:]]` resolves, no unresolved terms. Review history: Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#2, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#3, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#4.

title: Add the VDC (verifiable delegation credential) as a DTG edge credential
body:
## Problem

All six credential types in WD01 are **attestations** — each states that something is true about the graph, and a verifier evaluates it as a claim. Not one of them establishes that one entity may **act in another's name**. The VIC comes closest, but it is onboarding-shaped: its subject is by definition not yet in the graph, it is short-lived, and §Security says treat it as single-use.

Meanwhile delegation is already assumed by the specification's own vocabulary, with nothing to express it:

- `spec/terms-definitions/persona.md` — an identity controlled by the person "or their delegate"
- `spec/terms-definitions/personal_network_vault.md` — a person "may sometimes choose to delegate use of their credentials or keys to a VTA"
- `spec/intro.md` — AI agents are first-class DTG nodes, and an Agent Card VDS is planned

So today we can say "person P and agent A have a relationship" (VRC), but not "A may act in P's name, for these acts, until this date, and P can withdraw it."

## Delegation, not authority

The VDC is deliberately confined to **delegation**, and the PR adds an informative subsection, *Delegation and Authority*, saying so:

| Question | Answered by | The act is attributed to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| May this party do this thing, as itself? | authority — not defined in this specification | the party itself |
| May this party act in another's name? | delegation — the VDC | the entity in whose name it acts |

Neither implies the other. A service granted access to a person's mailbox may read that mail as itself; it has not thereby been appointed to send mail in that person's name. Conversely, a delegate appointed to correspond in a person's name holds that appointment whether or not it has access to any particular mailbox — and where it has not, the appointment gets it nowhere.

Two consequences are stated normatively:

- **A VDC never supplies authority.** A delegate cannot do in the delegator's name what the delegator could not do itself. A verifier must settle both questions separately, and a valid VDC is never on its own sufficient grounds to proceed (Security Considerations item 9).
- **The word "authority" is left free.** If the WG later wants a verifiable authority credential, it can be defined without reinterpreting the VDC or contending with it for the same semantic ground.

The subsection ends with a *when to use a VDC* test in the same style as the spec's existing credential/artifact test: **ask whose name the act is performed in.** The actor's own → a question of authority, not this credential. Another entity's, with the act attributed to that entity → delegation, and the VDC is what establishes it.

## How a delegation composes with authority

A second informative subsection answers the question a reviewer asks immediately after the first: if a VDC is not authority, does the delegate need authority of its own, or has the delegator handed its own over?

Neither. **A VDC moves the question; it does not answer it.** A verifier substitutes the delegator for the delegate and then asks the question it would have asked of the delegator directly. Three checks, each independent:

1. **Is this the delegate, and may it act in the delegator's name for this act?** — the VDC, plus chain and invocation binding. Defined here.
2. **May the delegator perform this act?** — membership, governance, an IDVC, a permission credential, verifier policy. Not defined here, and a VDC does not influence its outcome.
3. **Must the delegate independently qualify?** — a governance determination, now stated as such in §Governance Considerations.

The reach of a delegation is the **intersection** of what the delegator may do and what the VDC chain appoints the delegate for — never the union, and never more than either. Three consequences are spelled out:

- **Nothing the delegator holds is copied to the delegate.** A credential issued to the delegator stays the delegator's; the issuer's assurance about the delegator does not extend to the delegate, and a delegator cannot re-issue what it was itself issued. Delegation is a statement about who may speak in one's name, not a transfer of anything received.
- **Withdrawing the delegator's own permission stops the delegate immediately**, without revoking the VDC, because check 2 is evaluated at the time of the act. Revoking the VDC and withdrawing the underlying permission are different remedies with different reach.
- **A `scope` may exceed what the delegator itself may do**, which is not an error given that permissions change over the life of a durable appointment. Verifiers MUST NOT treat it as conferring anything beyond check 2; issuers SHOULD NOT do it.

This also rules out the alternative reading — a VDC as a container the delegator fills with its own permissions and hands over. That would make every issued authorization transferable by its holder, break the issuer's revocation reach, and attribute the act to the delegate rather than the delegator, which is the opposite of what delegation means.

## Why a new type rather than an existing one

Each overload fails, and the failures are informative:

- **VEC** — its `endorsement` object is community-defined and the spec explicitly says verifiability applies to the signature "not to the truth of the assertions." Putting representation inside a container whose stated semantics are *unverified opinion* means a verifier cannot distinguish "is good at Rust" from "may act as me."
- **VIC** — the least-bad overload, but its rules are terminal and onboarding-shaped, per above. Reusing it would mean redefining it.
- **VRC + a relationship-type field** — VRC currently carries no payload beyond `issuer` and `credentialSubject.id`. Adding semantics changes it from a bare edge to a typed one, which cuts against the ZKP predicate story, and imposes the bidirectional-pair requirement and the "new unique R-DID per counterparty" MUST on something inherently asymmetric.

The underlying reason is that a verifier evaluates an attestation by asking whether it is *true*. Representation asks something else — whether this party may stand in for that one, for this act, right now — and answering it requires scope containment, chain resolution, invocation binding and timely revocation. A distinct type string is what forces a verifier onto that path rather than the claim-evaluation one.

## What this PR does

Adds `DelegationCredential` (**VDC**) as a seventh concrete subtype and third edge credential.

**Applies the specification's own test.** §Credentials versus Trust Task Artifacts splits delegation cleanly, and the PR states this explicitly:

- the **grant** — "P appointed A to act in its name, for scope S, until T" — is true standing alone → credential, defined here
- the **invocation** — "A is acting in P's name, now, to do X" — is meaningful only in-exchange → trust task artifact, left to the DTG Core Trust Task Protocols spec

**Edge, with consent.** A grant plus a matching acceptance forms the edge, consistent with VRC/VMC pairing. A grant alone establishes what the delegator appointed, not what the delegate agreed to. This is the same consent question as #8 / #12 and is defined here in the same shape, without pre-empting that discussion.

**The machinery the six types do not have:**

- `delegation.scope` (REQUIRED, non-empty) — the acts the delegate may perform in the delegator's name; vocabulary governed by the VTC/VTN, exactly as VEC's `endorsement` is
- `delegation.parent` / `maxDepth` — attenuation-only re-delegation; a chain must resolve to a root delegation issued by the principal in whose name the acts would ultimately be performed. `parent` reuses the VWC `digest` encoding (SHA-256 over JCS) rather than introducing a second convention
- **Invocation binding** — a VDC is not a bearer token; the delegate must demonstrate key control at request time
- `validUntil` REQUIRED — an appointment with no expiry cannot be reasoned about by a verifier that cannot reach the delegator
- `credentialStatus` REQUIRED — see the note below

**Security considerations added:** misreading a VDC as a claim, treating a delegation as a permission, chain escalation, revocation latency, bearer use, and personhood laundering. The last is worth flagging on its own: a PHC asserts one membership per real person, and because a delegate's acts are attributable to the delegator, a verifier that cannot distinguish the two may credit several agents of one person as several people.

**Privacy considerations added:** delegation correlation (prefer R-DIDs), and scope terms as identifiers.

**Prior art:** ZCAP-LD and UCAN are cited in an informative subsection. The VDC reuses their *mechanics* — attenuation, root resolution, invocation binding — while noting the semantics differ: those models chain permissions, the VDC chains representation. It expresses those mechanics natively rather than embedding an opaque token, because scope is precisely the payload holders need to prove over in zero knowledge.

## Note on `credentialStatus`

`credentialStatus` currently appears **nowhere** in the specification. §Security Considerations tells verifiers to "check applicable revocation status via the governing trust registry," but no property tells them where to look. For attestations that is survivable; for a delegation — where revocation is the delegator's only means of withdrawing an appointment already made — it is not.

This PR therefore makes `credentialStatus` REQUIRED on the VDC only, and deliberately does not touch §Base Structure. The spec-wide question is worth its own issue and I'm happy to raise it separately.

## Also updated

Abstract, intro, taxonomy diagram and type hierarchy, `dtg_edge_credential` term (two subtypes → three), `specs.json` description, and a new `verifiable_delegation_credential` term definition. `CONTEXT.md` gains VDC and delegation-vs-authority language entries.

Renders clean with `npm run render`: no unresolved term references, all JSON examples parse, and the only dangling definitions reported are the five pre-existing ones.

## Open questions for the WG

1. **Scope vocabulary** — left entirely to VTC/VTN governance, mirroring VEC. Should the core spec instead define a minimal baseline so cross-community delegation is meaningful?
2. **A companion authority credential** — this PR reserves the ground rather than filling it. Is a verifiable authority credential wanted, and if so should the two be specified together so the boundary is drawn once?
3. **Delegate eligibility** — check 3 above is left to governance. Should the core spec instead take a position, e.g. requiring that a delegate acting within a community hold a VMC of its own?
4. **Acceptance strictness** — this draft requires the acceptance for a *complete edge* but lets a verifier rely on a grant alone where delegate consent isn't material. Should acceptance be unconditionally REQUIRED?
5. **`maxDepth` default** — this draft prohibits re-delegation when `maxDepth` is absent. Fail-closed seems right; confirming it is intended.
6. **ZKP constructions** — a delegation predicate is added to the list in §Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure, but the constructions themselves are not worked out. Likely interacts with #9.
7. **Naming** — VDC is free, but sits close to VDS (verifiable data structure). Worth a look.

Opened as a draft for WG discussion — happy to split the `credentialStatus` point out, or to restructure if the group would rather see delegation land in a companion specification.

title: fix(logs): identify the listener behind a lifecycle line, not just its name
body:
## Problem

A report of a listener connecting and disconnecting repeatedly, with an activity log in which every line reads:

```
[11:49:28] Listener 'dids.firstperson.dev/@geoffturk' connected
[11:49:28] WARNING: Listener 'dids.firstperson.dev/@geoffturk' cycling rapidl…
[11:49:28] Listener 'dids.firstperson.dev/@geoffturk' disconnected
[11:49:22] Listener 'dids.firstperson.dev/@geoffturk' connected
…
[11:04:33] Listener 'did:webvh:Qmaye5WLSxpCXraiu...' connected
```

Nothing in that log can say whether it is one listener cycling or several reconnecting independently, because the lines carry no identity — only a name.

**A name is not an identity.** `resolve_did_to_display` is many-to-one by construction: a contact alias or a verified agent name can stand for more than one DID, and a relationship R-DID deliberately resolves *through* to its peer's persona name. Two distinct listeners can render byte-identically.

It also changes under the reader. A listener that comes up before the background agent-name sweep lands is logged as a truncated DID, and minutes later as a name — visible in the log above, where the same listener appears as a DID at 11:04:33 and as a name from 11:16 on. The log appears to switch subject exactly when the sweep completes, which reads as *"this started when we began using an agent name"*.

## Fix

Every line that names a listener now carries the id it resolved from — abbreviated beside the name in the summary, in full in the detail behind `Enter`, alongside what it displayed as. The parenthetical is added only when a name was actually substituted, so an unnamed listener is not printed twice. `format_lifecycle_log` returns a summary/detail pair rather than a `String`.

A disconnect carrying no transport error now says "no transport error reported" rather than rendering as a bare "disconnected" — which was identical to a drop whose cause simply was not captured. Telling a clean close from an unexplained loss is the distinction R6.4 asks for.

**This changes what the log can tell you. It changes no connection behaviour.**

## On the underlying churn

Worth stating plainly, because this PR does not address it and should not be read as if it does:

* **Agent names are not in the connection path.** Every use of `Config::agent_name_for` is display-only — panels, log lines, join summaries. Nothing keys a transport, listener, session or identity by name, so resolving one cannot cause a reconnect.
* **The cadence does not match the agent-name sweep.** The sweep ticks every 300 s and only re-resolves entries past `AGENT_NAME_TTL` (24 h), so after the first successful lookup a DID is not touched again for a day. In the reported log, drops cluster on a **~14 min 58 s** period (11:16:33 → 11:31:31 → 11:46:29, and the same spacing for the other two phases), each cluster being a short burst of 2–3 drop/reconnect pairs that then settles. A ~15-minute period is the mediator access-token lifetime, not anything in this repo.
* The two `cycling rapidly` warnings correspond to same-id drops 7 s apart, inside the 10 s `CYCLING_WINDOW`.

So the likely subject is reconnect-on-token-refresh in the messaging layer, and the next step is a debug log (`OPENVTC_DEBUG_LOG`) covering one full cluster — the `checking auth expiry` lines will confirm or kill it. This PR is what makes that log interpretable: with ids on every line, "one listener burst-reconnecting every 15 minutes" and "three listeners on staggered schedules" stop looking the same.

## Tests

The name and the id both appear in the summary and the full id in the detail; two listeners sharing a name render differently in both; an unnamed listener does not repeat its id; a no-error drop says so; a lagged-stream notice still identifies no listener.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` — all green.

Note: **Cargo Deny** will fail here as it does on main and on #230 — RUSTSEC-2026-0258 (h2 < 0.4.16), published after these branches were cut and unrelated to any of them.

Changelog

## `vta-webvh`

## [0.1.10](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-webvh-v0.1.9...vta-webvh-v0.1.10) — 2026-08-18 ### Fixed - **webvh**: Read agent-name createdAt in both shapes the host sends ([#999](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/999)) * fix(webvh): read agent-name createdAt in both shapes the host sends A DID with at least one agent name could not be listed over DIDComm. The whole task failed with `agent-name list response parse error: invalid type: string "2026-08-18T08:58:13Z", expected u64`, which reached the operator as an internal error from a `set` that had in fact succeeded — the name was already in the DID document while the UI reported failure and showed an empty registry. `AgentNameEntryWire` is documented as the shape of the REST `GET /api/dids/{mnemonic}` `agentNames` array, where `createdAt` is Unix seconds as a number, and `webvh_didcomm::list_agent_names` reuses it to parse the DIDComm listing — where it is not. The published payload schema for `did-management/agent-name/list/0.1` types `createdAt` as `"string"` with `"format": "date-time"`, and the host projects it that way (affinidi-webvh-service, `did-hosting-control/src/messaging.rs`). Both producers are right. The same host emits *both* shapes: its DID record projection serialises the stored registry (numbers) while the list verb answers to the spec (strings), so one shape cannot simply be declared wrong. The consumer is the single place that sees both, so the wire type now accepts either and normalises to seconds — the VTA relays a `u64` outward in the canonical `AgentNameEntry`, so an RFC3339 input is converted rather than propagated. A third shape is a genuine contract break and still fails, quoting what arrived so it can be told apart from an unreachable host (R6.4). `chrono` moves from dev-dependencies to dependencies for the conversion. It was already in the build graph via `vta-service`.

title: fix(logs): identify the listener behind a lifecycle line, not just its name (#231)
body:
fix(logs): identify the listener behind a lifecycle line, not just its name (#231)

A report of a listener connecting and disconnecting repeatedly came with
an activity log in which every line read `Listener
'dids.firstperson.dev/@geoffturk' …`. Nothing in the log could say
whether that was one listener cycling or several reconnecting
independently, because the line carried no identity — only a name.

A name is not an identity. `resolve_did_to_display` is many-to-one by
construction: a contact alias or a verified agent name can stand for more
than one DID, and a relationship R-DID deliberately resolves *through* to
its peer's persona name. Two distinct listeners can therefore render
byte-identically. It also changes under the reader: a listener that
starts up before the background agent-name sweep lands is logged as a
truncated DID and then, minutes later, as a name — so the log appears to
switch subject at the moment the sweep completes, which reads as "this
started when we began using an agent name".

Every line that names a listener now carries the id it resolved from:
abbreviated beside the name in the summary (only when a name was actually
substituted, so an unnamed listener is not printed twice), and in full in
the detail behind `Enter`, alongside what it displayed as. The id is what
correlates with the mediator's own logs; the name is only what makes the
line readable.

`format_lifecycle_log` returns a summary/detail pair rather than a
`String`, so the runtime loop routes it through `log_detailed`.

A disconnect carrying no transport error now says "no transport error
reported" instead of rendering as a bare "disconnected" — identical to a
drop whose cause was not captured. Telling a clean close from an
unexplained loss is exactly the distinction R6.4 asks for.

This changes what the log can tell you; it does not change any
connection behaviour.

Tests: the name and the id both appear; two listeners sharing a name
render differently in both summary and detail; an unnamed listener does
not repeat its id; a no-error drop says so; a lagged-stream notice still
identifies no listener.

Gate: cargo fmt --all; cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D
warnings; cargo doc --workspace --no-deps (no warnings); cargo test
--workspace (all green).

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(webvh): read agent-name createdAt in both shapes the host sends
body:
## Problem

A DID with at least one agent name could not be listed over DIDComm. The whole task failed with:

```
agent-name list response parse error: invalid type: string "2026-08-18T08:58:13Z", expected u64
```

which reached the operator as an internal error from a `set` that had in fact **succeeded** — the name was already in the DID document while the UI reported failure and showed an empty registry. Empty registries parsed fine, so this only appeared *after* a successful claim.

## Why both producers are right

`AgentNameEntryWire` is documented as the shape of the REST `GET /api/dids/{mnemonic}` `agentNames` array, where `createdAt` is Unix seconds as a number. `webvh_didcomm::list_agent_names` reuses it to parse the DIDComm listing — where it is not: the published payload schema for `did-management/agent-name/list/0.1` types `createdAt` as `"string"` with `"format": "date-time"`, and the host projects it that way (`affinidi-webvh-service`, `did-hosting-control/src/messaging.rs`, since 2026-07-29).

Neither side is wrong, and the mismatch is not fixable by picking one. The **same host emits both shapes**: its DID-record projection serialises the stored registry (numbers) while the list verb answers to the spec (strings). The consumer is the single place that sees both.

## Fix

The wire type accepts either and normalises to seconds. The VTA relays a `u64` outward in the canonical `AgentNameEntry`, so an RFC3339 input is converted rather than propagated — a deliberate asymmetry between what this reads and what it emits.

A third shape is a genuine contract break and still fails, quoting what arrived so it can be told apart from an unreachable host (R6.4).

`chrono` moves from dev-dependencies to dependencies for the conversion. It was already in the build graph via `vta-service`.

## Tests

* Both wire shapes decode (epoch number; RFC3339 string).
* An offset timestamp normalises to the same instant as its UTC twin.
* A two-entry listing decodes as an array — the shape `list_agent_names` actually deserialises.
* An uninterpretable timestamp fails with the offending value in the message.

`cargo test -p vta-webvh` (53) and `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` (823) pass; `cargo clippy -p vta-webvh --all-targets` is clean. (The workspace has a pre-existing `dead_code` warning in `vti-common` unrelated to this change, which trips a `-D warnings` run.)

## Not covered

No test drives the DIDComm listing end to end against a host. The parse is unit-covered at the type, but the producer/consumer pairing that broke here is still only checked by hand — the same gap that let this ship.

## Deployment

The fix reaches clients through a `vta-service` release and redeploy; consumers such as OpenVTC need no dependency change.

title: fix(vta): load the VIC list off the loop, and stop dropping keys silently
body:
## Problem

Two ways the VTA Service panel looked broken, both rooted in the state-handler loop servicing actions serially with inline `.await`s.

**Tab lagged by a network round-trip.** The Tab handler sent `VicRefresh` and *then* `VicFocusToggle`. `refresh_vics` awaited `cred_vault_query` inline — a trust task with a 30 s SDK timeout — so the focus change, a two-line in-memory mutation, could not be applied until the vault answered. The delay was invisible and asymmetric: Tab back off the VIC list sends no refresh and was always instant.

**`g` did nothing at all, for three independent reasons** — and a restart "fixed" each one differently, which is what made the report so hard to pin down:

* It lived in the DID-list focus arm, so pressing it with the VIC list focused was swallowed with no action, no state change and no message.
* `did_selected_index` was never clamped when the persona list was rebuilt. Every list-scoped key is guarded on `did_selected < did_count`, so a stale index disabled them all while drawing no cursor to show why. Restarting worked because the index starts at 0.
* Both lists drew their focus affordance from `state.focus` alone, so a panel the keyboard could not reach still announced "◀ focus" and advertised its verbs — while every one of those keys was discarded (content keys are only routed when the content panel is selected).

## Fix

The listing runs as a background dispatch (`DispatchDomain::Vic`), so the loop only starts it: focus moves on the next frame and the list fills in when it lands. **Both** loops get it — the degraded (State-A) loop gains a dispatch channel of its own, because an account with no community lives on this screen and shouldn't be the one that feels slow.

`spawn_vic_refresh` now owns every load, so the mutation paths no longer re-list inline and no stale in-flight result can overwrite a fresh one. Two ordering rules fall out of that:

* A request arriving while the vault is busy is **deferred, not dropped**. The in-flight query predates whatever prompted the new one, so discarding it would leave a just-archived VIC rendered as active until someone refreshed by hand.
* A listing whose `include_inactive` no longer matches the panel is discarded on arrival — `i` was pressed while it was in flight, and the refresh queued behind it carries the right question.

The panel says when a query is in flight. "No invitation credentials" is a claim about the vault and can only be made once the vault answers.

`g` moves up to the focus-independent keys beside `n` and `a` (the selection it acts on is the DID list's, which Tab does not move), the persona selection is clamped on every sync, and the focus affordance now distinguishes three states rather than two — including "the panel itself isn't focused", where it points at the key that actually helps.

Finally, a claim that succeeds and a reload that then fails no longer renders "No agent names yet." above "Applied, but could not reload the list" — the prominent half said the opposite of what happened, for a name the DID document already carried. The overlay marks the registry unknown instead. (The underlying reload failure is a VTA-side contract skew, fixed separately in `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`: OpenVTC needs no dependency change for it.)

## Tests

* Refresh-outcome apply: swaps the listing in and clears the loading flag; clamps a selection past the end; drops a listing for a superseded filter; a failed query keeps the previous list and logs the reason.
* The defer-don't-drop guard across all three outcomes (no session / free / busy).
* The persona-selection clamp on sync.
* `g` from either list; Tab ordering in both directions.
* The panel's unfocused affordance and its loading state.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` — all green.

## Not covered

The agent-name manager's own list still runs inline on the loop (60 s timeout). It shows a Loading overlay, so it is visible rather than mysterious, but it still parks the loop while it runs.

Changelog

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.25.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.24.0...vta-sdk-v0.25.0) — 2026-08-17 ### Added - **vta-keys**: Add non-extractable internal signing keys ([#995](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/995)) An ordinary VTA key is BIP-32 derived, so anyone holding the 24-word mnemonic can reconstruct it offline. That is what makes the VTA recoverable, and equally what makes "the operator cannot obtain this key" false — the second limb of what eIDAS calls sole control. An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it. Deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path. That path wraps its secrets under a KEK derived from the master seed (derive_kek(seed, salt)), so a non-extractable flag on it would be decorative: the boundary it claims to enforce has already been walked around. Internal keys get their own keyspace, INTERNAL_KEYS, with no seed involvement at any point, and that keyspace is in EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP by design — a backup carrying it would be an export of keys the VTA promises never to export, and restoring it elsewhere would clone a signer. Refused for did:webvh log entries, enforced in code rather than left to guidance. WebVH is append-only and each entry is authorised by the update key the previous entry named; an unrecoverable update key means that if storage is lost the DID can never be updated again by anyone, permanently, and every integration pinned to it is stranded. Credentials can be re-issued, an append-only identity log cannot. Internal keys remain fine as a signing verificationMethod inside a published document, where loss costs the ability to produce new signatures rather than control of the identity. The export refusal is not a permission check — admin is not a bypass, because the value of the origin is that no caller holds this power. There are two refusals (an early return and an in-match arm); removing either leaves the other, and removing both does not compile, since the match over KeyOrigin becomes non-exhaustive. An export path cannot silently reopen. Operator surfaces carry the cost prominently: `pnm keys create --internal` prints what is lost and requires the operator to type a confirmation phrase rather than mash y, the response repeats the warning, and docs/02-vta/ internal-keys.md covers when to use one, what actually protects it (enclave measurement + KMS, not a mnemonic), and the two things that genuinely destroy it. - **vta-service**: Present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP ([#993](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/993)) * feat(vta-service)!: present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP Completes mdoc support. A VTA could receive, verify and store an mdoc; it could not present one. This is the last piece, and it needed three things the other formats do not. An OID4VP session on the query wire. An mdoc's holder binding is a DeviceAuth signature over an ISO 18013-7 SessionTranscript, whose handover is [clientId, responseUri, nonce, mdocGeneratedNonce]. Two of those exist only in an OID4VP exchange, so a verifier that wants an mdoc supplies them; QueryBody gains an optional oid4vp_session carrying OID4VP's own field names, so a verifier can copy them out of its authorization request unrenamed. Absent, an mdoc is not offered at all rather than offered unbound. A DeviceAuth over invented handover values verifies nowhere and, worse, looks bound. That is what makes the VTA recoverable, and equally what makes "the operator cannot obtain this key" false — the second limb of what eIDAS calls sole control. An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it. Deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path. That path wraps its secrets under a KEK derived from the master seed (derive_kek(seed, salt)), so a non-extractable flag on it would be decorative: the boundary it claims to enforce has already been walked around. Refused for did:webvh log entries, enforced in code rather than left to guidance. WebVH is append-only and each entry is authorised by the update key the previous entry named; an unrecoverable update key means that if storage is lost the DID can never be updated again by anyone, permanently, and every integration pinned to it is stranded. Credentials can be re-issued, an append-only identity log cannot. Internal keys remain fine as a signing verificationMethod inside a published document, where loss costs the ability to produce new signatures rather than control of the identity. The export refusal is not a permission check — admin is not a bypass, because the value of the origin is that no caller holds this power. There are two refusals (an early return and an in-match arm); removing either leaves the other, and removing both does not compile, since the match over KeyOrigin becomes non-exhaustive. An export path cannot silently reopen. title: DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its taskContext binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)
body:
# DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its `taskContext` binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)

## Context

[trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#11](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/11) flagged that DTG Core Credentials placed normative requirements on `taskContext`-bearing credentials (outcome evidence, terminal states, etc.) that depended on "the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification" — which doesn't exist yet, so the requirements were untestable.

Resolution ([dtgwg-cred-spec#15](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/15)) restructures that section to depend only on mechanisms **already defined in this framework's current editor's draft**, rather than on any future spec:

- **Terminal state** = presence of a `#response`-variant document ([§4.4.1](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#441-request-and-response-variants)) or a `trust-task-error` document ([§8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#8-error-responses)), correlated by `threadId` ([§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member)).
- **Outcome integrity** = the existing per-specification `proof`-required declaration ([§7.3 item 8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Outcome artifact structure** = the existing per-specification `#response` payload schema ([§7.3 item 7.6](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Evidence discovery / retrieval authorization / confidentiality** — sidestepped for cred-spec's v1.0 by requiring the outcome document to travel *with* the credential presentation, rather than be discovered/retrieved asynchronously by a verifier who wasn't party to the original exchange. (This framework's bilateral, transport-bound request/response model doesn't naturally support that kind of later, third-party retrieval, so cred-spec isn't relying on it.)

cred-spec now requires that any Trust Task specification a VTC/VTN designates as the referent of a DTG credential's `taskContext` — a "qualifying" specification — declare `proof` REQUIRED on its response/error variants and define a `#response` schema (or rely on `trust-task-error`). That's it; no framework behavior change required for this to work.

**No action needed on your side for cred-spec's fix to land.** Filing this mainly so you're aware of the cross-reference (per the coordination cred-spec's Governance Considerations already calls for between the two task forces), and to flag one small, genuinely optional framework enhancement that would make part of this more robust.

## Optional ask: let a Trust Task specification declare `threadId` as REQUIRED-and-unique

cred-spec needs `taskContext` (its own name for a `threadId`) to reliably name *one specific* exchange. Right now `threadId` is framework-wide `MAY`, and [§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member) is explicit that it "carries no normative validation semantics" — no presence guarantee, no uniqueness guarantee, and consumers can't reject on it.

cred-spec works around this by putting the uniqueness burden entirely on DTG *issuers* (its own conformance target), which is sufficient for cred-spec's purposes but means the framework's own consumer-side machinery can't enforce it — a misbehaving issuer's threadId reuse isn't independently rejectable the way, say, a missing required `proof` is (`proofRequired`, [§7.2 item 7](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

Proposal: add a declarable property to [§7.3](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements), mirroring item 8's Proof requirement pattern:

> **Thread requirement** — an explicit statement of whether `threadId` is OPTIONAL or REQUIRED for documents implementing the specification, together (where REQUIRED) with the uniqueness scope it MUST satisfy (e.g., "unique per exchange instance for the life of the specification's use"). A conforming consumer MUST reject a document lacking a REQUIRED `threadId` with `malformedRequest`, consistent with the existing `recipient`-required pattern ([§7.2 item 5](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

This is additive only — it doesn't touch `threadId`'s existing general-purpose, loosely-specified behavior for specifications that don't opt in. It would let a future DTG-ceremony Trust Task specification (or any other specification with the same need) get framework-level enforcement instead of relying on the depending spec's issuer-side discipline alone.

Happy to draft this as a PR here if it's wanted, or to help co-author a worked-example Trust Task specification for a DTG ceremony (e.g. relationship witnessing) satisfying the "qualifying" profile above, as a joint appendix in either repo — similar in spirit to your own Appendix A. Let us know which is useful.

title: fix(acl): reuse live ATM profile for mediator ACL self-provisioning
body:
## Problem

On a mediator that applies a restrictive per-account ACL default (ExplicitAllow inbox mode), an agent and its DIDComm clients could appear connected yet never receive forwarded messages. Two root causes:

1. **Duplicate-channel eviction.** ACL self-provisioning opened a *second* WebSocket for the same DID right after the messaging connection was established. Mediators enforce one socket per DID and evict the newer connection as `duplicate-channel`, so the ACL trust task timed out silently. The inbox stayed ExplicitAllow and every forwarded message was dropped.

2. **Trust-task API mismatch.** Newer SDKs provision ACLs via the `account_update` trust task, which older mediators do not implement — they only understand the retired `acl/set` task. Against those mediators the update was rejected and the ACL was never set.

## Fix

- Add `set_client_acl_with_profile`, which reuses the already-connected `Arc<ATMProfile>` instead of spawning a new socket; update the agent startup and the DIDComm-connect call sites to use it.
- Add a dual-API fallback in the shared `apply_acl_set`: try `account_update` first, and on rejection fall back to a raw `acl/set` exchange built from the trust-tasks types. The fallback uses `wait_for_response=true` so the mediator's reply returns directly over the live WebSocket rather than via the (still-closed) forwarded inbox.
- Provision the client ACL in `TrustPingSession` (blocking variant) before the first ping, so an ExplicitAllow mediator can forward the ping response back.
- Keep `set_client_acl_on_connection` as a public API for callers without a pre-built profile.

## Compatibility

Forward-compatible with mediators that implement `account_update`; backward-compatible with 0.17.x mediators that only implement `acl/set`.

## Testing

Verified end-to-end with a local strict-ACL harness that reproduces the restrictive (ExplicitAllow) per-account posture against a did:webvh agent + did:webvh mediator + DIDComm client. Round-trip `keys list` / `acl list` / `keys create` all succeed over DIDComm (previously blocked). Both the agent and client sides carry the fallback.

title: chore(deps): take trust-tasks 0.9, vta-sdk 0.25 and did-git-sign 0.4.5
body:
**The last repo in the fleet still resolving `trust-tasks-rs` 0.6.5.**

It could not move until now: `did-git-sign` 0.4.4 required `vta-sdk ^0.24`, which required `trust-tasks-rs ^0.6`, so openvtc's graph was pinned by a dependency two repos away. VGI 0.4.5, published today, closes that.

## What moves

| requirement | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.5 | **0.8** |
| `vta-sdk` | 0.24 | **0.25** |
| `vta-service` (**dev**-dependency) | 0.15 | **0.17** |

`did-git-sign`'s `"0.4.3"` caret already admitted 0.4.5; the lockfile carries it.

## The dev-dependency is why the shipped-graph check isn't enough

`cargo tree -d -e normal,build` was **clean** while `-e normal,build,dev` still showed two `vta-sdk` and two `trust-tasks-rs`.

`openvtc-core` dev-depends on `vta-service` for the in-process `MockVta` the bootstrap e2e runs against, and that pin was a line behind. Its own comment states the rule — *"track this with the vta-sdk major"* — and 0.17 is the line built against `vta-sdk` 0.25, as 0.15 was against 0.23. I extended that comment's version ledger rather than rewriting it.

## One source change, seven sites

`CreateKeyRequest` gained `internal` (VTI #995), so the literals in `state_handler/relationship_actions.rs` and `state_handler/setup_sequence/vta.rs` name it.

**`None` is deliberate.** Absent is today's behaviour; `Some(true)` mints a CSPRNG key that is never exported, excluded from backup, and **cannot be recovered from the mnemonic or otherwise**. That is not a property to acquire by filling in a compiler error.

## Nothing else broke — and that was by prior design

This workspace consumes `trust-task-error` documents and emits none, and it was already written version-agnostically: a `TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_PREFIX` constant plus `is_trust_task_error_type`'s `starts_with`, with a test asserting the match holds across versions.

The framework's move to `trust-task-error/0.5` therefore needs **no change here**. The `0.1`/`0.2` literals in that module are the test proving exactly that, and are left alone.

## Comments updated

Both `Cargo.toml` blocks now record this move rather than the last one, including a new note that the duplicate check must cover the **dev** graph — the failure above would have been missed by the shipped-graph check alone.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — **710 pass, 0 fail**
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — no errors
- `cargo tree -d -e normal,build` **and** `-e normal,build,dev` — neither lists `trust-tasks-rs`, `trust-tasks-capability-client`, `vta-sdk`, `vta-service`, `vti-common` or `affinidi-tdk`

title: vta-service-v0.17.0
body:
### Added

- **vta-keys**: Add non-extractable internal signing keys ([#995](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/995))

An ordinary VTA key is BIP-32 derived, so anyone holding the 24-word mnemonic
  can reconstruct it offline. That is what makes the VTA recoverable, and equally
  what makes "the operator cannot obtain this key" false — the second limb of what
  eIDAS calls sole control.

  An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and
  is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it.

  Deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path. That path wraps its secrets
  under a KEK derived from the master seed (derive_kek(seed, salt)), so a
  non-extractable flag on it would be decorative: the boundary it claims to
  enforce has already been walked around. Internal keys get their own keyspace,
  INTERNAL_KEYS, with no seed involvement at any point, and that keyspace is in
  EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP by design — a backup carrying it would be an export of keys
  the VTA promises never to export, and restoring it elsewhere would clone a
  signer.

  Refused for did:webvh log entries, enforced in code rather than left to
  guidance. WebVH is append-only and each entry is authorised by the update key
  the previous entry named; an unrecoverable update key means that if storage is
  lost the DID can never be updated again by anyone, permanently, and every
  integration pinned to it is stranded. Credentials can be re-issued, an
  append-only identity log cannot. Internal keys remain fine as a signing
  verificationMethod inside a published document, where loss costs the ability to
  produce new signatures rather than control of the identity.

  The export refusal is not a permission check — admin is not a bypass, because
  the value of the origin is that no caller holds this power. There are two
  refusals (an early return and an in-match arm); removing either leaves the other,
  and removing both does not compile, since the match over KeyOrigin becomes
  non-exhaustive. An export path cannot silently reopen.

  Operator surfaces carry the cost prominently: `pnm keys create --internal`
  prints what is lost and requires the operator to type a confirmation phrase
  rather than mash y, the response repeats the warning, and docs/02-vta/
  internal-keys.md covers when to use one, what actually protects it (enclave
  measurement + KMS, not a mnemonic), and the two things that genuinely destroy
  it.

- **vta-service**: Present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP ([#993](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/993))

* feat(vta-service)!: present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP

  Completes mdoc support. A VTA could receive, verify and store an mdoc; it could
  not present one. This is the last piece, and it needed three things the other
  formats do not.

  An OID4VP session on the query wire. An mdoc's holder binding is a DeviceAuth
  signature over an ISO 18013-7 SessionTranscript, whose handover is
  [clientId, responseUri, nonce, mdocGeneratedNonce]. Two of those exist only in
  an OID4VP exchange, so a verifier that wants an mdoc supplies them; QueryBody
  gains an optional oid4vp_session carrying OID4VP's own field names, so a
  verifier can copy them out of its authorization request unrenamed.

  Absent, an mdoc is not offered at all rather than offered unbound. A DeviceAuth
  over invented handover values verifies nowhere and, worse, looks bound. The gate
  lives in match_held so matchable and presentable stay the same set: a
  matched-but-unpresentable credential bails the entire vp_token, not just itself,
  taking every other credential the verifier legitimately asked for with it. A
  mutation removing the gate fails the test that pins this.

  Holder identity that is key-shaped. ConsentGrant.holder_did becomes
  HolderIdentity::{Subject, DeviceKey}: every other format names a subject DID,
  while an mdoc names a device key discovered at receive. Both resolve to a
  did:key because ConsentRecord::verify_proof binds the proof's
  verificationMethod to the data subject — the variant records provenance that
  would otherwise be silently lost, not a different kind of value.

  A P-256 consent receipt. The device key signs its own receipt under
  ecdsa-jcs-2019 (affinidi-data-integrity 0.7.10), where every other format uses
  eddsa-jcs-2022. Signing the receipt with some other key would break the
  verificationMethod binding above; that is why the cryptosuite was added upstream
  rather than worked around here.

  Presentation itself is not a present_single arm: an mdoc vp_token entry is
  base64url CBOR of a DeviceResponse, not a W3C VP object, so present_mdoc sits
  beside it. Selective disclosure is by omission — only the [namespace, element]
  paths the query asked for are included.

body:
### Added

- **vta-keys**: Add non-extractable internal signing keys ([#995](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/995))

An ordinary VTA key is BIP-32 derived, so anyone holding the 24-word mnemonic
  can reconstruct it offline. That is what makes the VTA recoverable, and equally
  what makes "the operator cannot obtain this key" false — the second limb of what
  eIDAS calls sole control.

  An internal key is generated from the system CSPRNG, has no derivation path, and
  is never returned by any surface. The VTA acts only as a signing oracle for it.

  Deliberately not a flag on the imported-key path. That path wraps its secrets
  under a KEK derived from the master seed (derive_kek(seed, salt)), so a
  non-extractable flag on it would be decorative: the boundary it claims to
  enforce has already been walked around. Internal keys get their own keyspace,
  INTERNAL_KEYS, with no seed involvement at any point, and that keyspace is in
  EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP by design — a backup carrying it would be an export of keys
  the VTA promises never to export, and restoring it elsewhere would clone a
  signer.

  Refused for did:webvh log entries, enforced in code rather than left to
  guidance. WebVH is append-only and each entry is authorised by the update key
  the previous entry named; an unrecoverable update key means that if storage is
  lost the DID can never be updated again by anyone, permanently, and every
  integration pinned to it is stranded. Credentials can be re-issued, an
  append-only identity log cannot. Internal keys remain fine as a signing
  verificationMethod inside a published document, where loss costs the ability to
  produce new signatures rather than control of the identity.

  The export refusal is not a permission check — admin is not a bypass, because
  the value of the origin is that no caller holds this power. There are two
  refusals (an early return and an in-match arm); removing either leaves the other,
  and removing both does not compile, since the match over KeyOrigin becomes
  non-exhaustive. An export path cannot silently reopen.

  Operator surfaces carry the cost prominently: `pnm keys create --internal`
  prints what is lost and requires the operator to type a confirmation phrase
  rather than mash y, the response repeats the warning, and docs/02-vta/
  internal-keys.md covers when to use one, what actually protects it (enclave
  measurement + KMS, not a mnemonic), and the two things that genuinely destroy
  it.

- **vta-service**: Present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP ([#993](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/993))

* feat(vta-service)!: present ISO mdoc credentials over OID4VP

  Completes mdoc support. A VTA could receive, verify and store an mdoc; it could
  not present one. This is the last piece, and it needed three things the other
  formats do not.

  An OID4VP session on the query wire. An mdoc's holder binding is a DeviceAuth
  signature over an ISO 18013-7 SessionTranscript, whose handover is
  [clientId, responseUri, nonce, mdocGeneratedNonce]. Two of those exist only in
  an OID4VP exchange, so a verifier that wants an mdoc supplies them; QueryBody
  gains an optional oid4vp_session carrying OID4VP's own field names, so a
  verifier can copy them out of its authorization request unrenamed.

  Absent, an mdoc is not offered at all rather than offered unbound. A DeviceAuth
  over invented handover values verifies nowhere and, worse, looks bound. The gate
  lives in match_held so matchable and presentable stay the same set: a
  matched-but-unpresentable credential bails the entire vp_token, not just itself,
  taking every other credential the verifier legitimately asked for with it. A
  mutation removing the gate fails the test that pins this.

  Holder identity that is key-shaped. ConsentGrant.holder_did becomes
  HolderIdentity::{Subject, DeviceKey}: every other format names a subject DID,
  while an mdoc names a device key discovered at receive. Both resolve to a
  did:key because ConsentRecord::verify_proof binds the proof's
  verificationMethod to the data subject — the variant records provenance that
  would otherwise be silently lost, not a different kind of value.

  A P-256 consent receipt. The device key signs its own receipt under
  ecdsa-jcs-2019 (affinidi-data-integrity 0.7.10), where every other format uses
  eddsa-jcs-2022. Signing the receipt with some other key would break the
  verificationMethod binding above; that is why the cryptosuite was added upstream
  rather than worked around here.

  Presentation itself is not a present_single arm: an mdoc vp_token entry is
  base64url CBOR of a DeviceResponse, not a W3C VP object, so present_mdoc sits
  beside it. Selective disclosure is by omission — only the [namespace, element]
  paths the query asked for are included.

title: chore(deps)!: track trust-tasks 0.9 across the workspace
body:
## What

Moves all five `trust-tasks-*` requirements plus `trust-tasks-capability-client` (0.5 → 0.8) together, and takes the `affinidi-messaging-*` releases built on 0.9 alongside them.

| dependency | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-https` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | 0.6 | **0.9** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.5 | **0.8** |
| `affinidi-messaging-sdk` (transitive) | 0.19.7 | 0.19.8 |
| `affinidi-messaging-mediator` (transitive) | 0.18.17 | 0.18.18 |

They move as one because `trust-tasks-rs`'s core types cross the public API of `-https` / `-didcomm` / `-proof` — a graph mixing majors does not type-check.

## What cost nothing

- **No `consume_inbound` call sites in this workspace**, so 0.9.0's new required `PayloadPolicy` argument does not reach us.
- **Nothing matches on `StandardCode`**, so 0.7.0's `#[non_exhaustive]` does not either.
- The `validate` feature stays enabled and unused, exactly as before.

## What did change: the error version on the wire

`trust-task-error` moved 0.3 → 0.4 → 0.5 upstream. Each step happened for the same reason the 0.3 step did — a new standard code the older payload schema's `code` enum does not list and whose extended-code pattern does not match, so a document carrying it would not validate as the older version. `0.4` carries `idConflict`, `0.5` carries `cancelled` (SPEC §8.3).

Both services hand-write that version on their **one unrouted path** — where there is no request document to reject from, and therefore no framework call to ask. Both were left naming `0.3` while `reject_with` stamped `0.5` on every *routed* rejection. One service emitting two versions is a trap for exactly the consumer that pins one of them.

**`unrouted_and_routed_errors_agree_on_the_type_uri` exists in both services to catch this, and it did.** The bump failed those two tests rather than shipping two dialects. That is the test doing its job; constants updated and their rationale extended.

## Fixture tidy-up (and why the census count was not raised)

Two in-`src` VTC test fixtures also named `0.3`. They now take the version from `framework_error_type_uri()` rather than repeating it, so they follow the emitter on the next bump instead of stranding a version behind.

That also keeps `trust_task_manifest`'s unpublished-URI census at **one** URI for the family. The census is deliberately exact so the debt can shrink but never grow unnoticed, and its own failure message says raising the expected count is the wrong fix — so I didn't.

**Backward acceptance of an older error document keeps its coverage:** `vtc-service/tests/registry_didcomm.rs` pins `0.1` on purpose and is left alone.

## Compatibility

Per SPEC §5.2 forward-minor compatibility, a consumer still pinned to `trust-task-error/0.3` SHOULD accept `0.5`. Marked `!` because this changes the version on the wire, not because any Rust signature moved.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — all suites pass, 0 failures
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo tree -d -e normal,build` lists **none** of `trust-tasks-rs`, `trust-tasks-capability-client`, `vta-sdk`, `vti-common`, `affinidi-tdk`
- `scripts/check-lockfile-self-pins.sh` — no self-pin
- **No `version =` field touched**, per RELEASING.md — versions are the Release PR's job

### Unrelated pre-existing breakage found while verifying

`cargo check --workspace --all-features --all-targets` fails in `vta-sdk/tests/provision_client_e2e.rs` (5 × `E0609`). **Not caused by this PR** — it reproduces on `main`. PR #949 (`fix(provisioning)!: relay the holder's bootstrap VP as raw JSON`) changed `ProvisionIntegrationRequest::request` to `serde_json::Value` on 2026-08-12 without updating that test, and no CI job builds `--all-features --all-targets`, so it went unnoticed. Left for a separate fix; flagging it here rather than folding it in.
