title: feat(framework): require a binding to justify any allowance to omit proof (§9.1.1)
body:
Closes #206.

## The gap

§4.7.1 lets a document omit `proof` where the transport provides end-to-end integrity and authentication between *producer* and *consumer*. §9.1 only **SHOULD**ed the security profile that establishes whether a given transport actually does. So a binding could rest an allowance on "the transport is authenticated" without stating which party is authenticated, how that principal becomes a VID, what an intermediary can do to the bytes, or where the guarantee stops.

§9.1.1 now requires a binding permitting omission to address **eight** properties, and to say explicitly where one doesn't apply rather than leaving it out. Two rules do most of the work:

- **Hop authentication is not producer authentication** where an intermediary can re-originate undetected. It tells a consumer who handed it the bytes, not who wrote them.
- **State the allowance per mode** where a transport has both an end-to-end mode and a relayed one — a single allowance overstates the weaker case.

**Silence is not permission.** A binding that doesn't address omission must not be read as permitting it. That clause isn't in the issue; I added it because the gap it closes was live — see `https/0.1` below.

## Audit of all seven published bindings

Only **`didcomm-v1/0.2`** targets framework 0.4, so it's the only binding the new MUST binds — the same targeting logic as §7.3 item 15 in #218.

| Binding | Target | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `tsp/0.1` | 0.2 | **Already conforms.** Per-mode table (direct / nested / non-nested routed) plus a §7 profile. The model the issue cited |
| `push/0.1` | 0.2 | **Already conforms** — states plainly that the channel provides no guarantee the framework relies on. Exactly the disclosure §9.1.1 asks for |
| `didcomm-v1/0.2` | **0.4** | **Bound. Fixed here** |
| `https/0.1` | 0.2 | Not bound, **fixed here anyway** — see below |
| `didcomm/0.1`, `didcomm/0.2`, `didcomm-v1/0.1` | 0.2–0.3 | Permit omission with an incomplete profile. Not bound; left for a hygiene sweep |

## `https/0.1` — the live gap

It had **no transport security profile at all**, while being the binding most likely to be read as providing one. "HTTPS with an `Authorization` header" sounds end-to-end, and it is — between the client and *whatever terminates TLS*.

The binding's own Abstract places TLS termination "by a reverse proxy or natively at the server" outside its scope, so it cannot say how many segments exist. Any terminating intermediary — proxy, load balancer, API gateway, mesh sidecar — sees plaintext and can re-originate the body undetectably. And identity comes from a **bearer token** mapped to a VID by a deployment-defined mechanism, with the binding explicitly making "no claim about token-revocation, audience-restriction, or replay protection."

So the honest content of its new §5 is that **this binding does not permit omission**, with the eight properties filled in to show why. A bearer token authenticates whoever presents it — the party that reached the terminator, not necessarily the party that composed the document.

## `didcomm-v1/0.2` — what was missing

Its §3 already handled attribution unusually well (v1 authenticates a bare verkey, not a DID; the three outcomes are already normative), so the new §6 adds the parts nobody had written down:

- A mediator **cannot** modify the inner authcrypt envelope undetected, but **can** drop, delay, reorder and **re-deliver** it.
- v1 provides **no replay protection at all**, and store-and-forward admits arbitrary delay.
- A key rotation the agent hasn't processed leaves a **superseded verkey still authenticating**.

The absent freshness guarantee makes §7.2 item 11 (from #223) load-bearing here: nothing in this transport stops the same document arriving twice, so a consumer treating mediated delivery as at-most-once is wrong on both a hostile replay and an ordinary mediator retry.

## Versioning

Prose only, **in place, no new binding versions** — all seven bindings are `draft` and §5.2's errata rule applies to them as to specifications. Section renumbering in both edited files, with internal anchors updated.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — 303 specs, unchanged.
- `npm run build` — passes, including `checkBindingRegistry()`; bindings synced to the website tree.
- Anchors verified: 61 in SPEC.md, plus all anchors in both edited bindings, resolve after renumbering.
- No spec, schema, or generated code touched — no library regeneration or version bump.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance, from a read of all seven bindings. Declared for symmetry with the originating issue.

title: Require transport bindings to justify any allowance to omit an in-band proof
body:
## Summary

§4.7.1 permits `proof` to be omitted when the transport already provides end-to-end integrity and authentication between the producer and consumer.

The current repository's transport bindings show that this can be specified carefully.

For example:

- the TSP binding distinguishes direct, nested-routed, and non-nested-routed cases and treats their producer-to-consumer security properties differently; and
- the DIDComm bindings distinguish cases where authenticated transport identity is actually attributable to the relevant party.

These are useful examples of the level of analysis required.

The framework-level requirement is weaker. §9 states that a transport protocol used for Trust Tasks **SHOULD** be accompanied by a transport binding, and §9.1 says a transport binding **SHOULD** specify its transport security profile, including integrity, authentication, confidentiality, and freshness guarantees.

Because those guarantees can determine whether the framework's in-band `proof` may be omitted, the security profile supporting that decision should be mandatory whenever a binding permits proof omission.

## Impact of the issue identified

A future binding could claim that its transport authentication is sufficient to omit `proof` without precisely defining:

- which entity is authenticated as the Trust Task producer;
- how that identity maps to a VID;
- whether intermediaries can modify or re-originate the document;
- how the intended consumer is bound;
- what freshness or replay guarantees exist; or
- where the actual end-to-end security boundary terminates.

This could make proof requirements transport-dependent in a way that is difficult for implementers to evaluate consistently.

The existing TSP and DIDComm bindings demonstrate that the problem is solvable. The framework should make that level of justification an interoperability requirement rather than optional binding guidance.

## Suggested path to resolution

Narrow the change to §9.1.

A transport binding that permits `proof` omission should be required to document the exact security properties on which that allowance depends.

At minimum, it should explain:

1. how the actual producer is authenticated;
2. how the authenticated transport principal maps to the Trust Task VID;
3. how the intended consumer is identified or bound;
4. how document integrity is preserved across intermediaries;
5. whether any intermediary can modify or re-originate the Trust Task;
6. what freshness/replay protection applies; and
7. any credential, key-status, or trust assumptions required by the binding.

The TSP and DIDComm binding language can serve as positive examples rather than requiring a new universal transport mechanism.

## Suggested normative text

Amend §9.1 along the following lines:

> A *transport binding* **MUST** specify its transport security profile where any framework security or identity requirement is derived from transport context.
>
> A transport binding that permits a *Trust Task document* to omit `proof` under §4.7.1 **MUST** specify the security properties that establish end-to-end integrity and authentication between the actual *producer* and *consumer*.
>
> That specification **MUST** describe:
>
> 1. the authenticated producer credential or transport principal;
> 2. the deterministic mapping from that principal to the VID used for framework identity comparison;
> 3. recipient identification or audience binding;
> 4. integrity protection across any intermediary capable of modifying or re-originating the document;
> 5. freshness or replay protection;
> 6. relevant credential, key-status, or revocation checks; and
> 7. any condition under which the transport ceases to provide producer-to-consumer end-to-end protection.
>
> A binding **MUST NOT** state that `proof` may be omitted solely because an individual transport hop is authenticated where an intermediary can modify or re-originate the Trust Task document without detection by the final consumer.

This change would make the existing binding discipline explicit without requiring the framework to mandate any particular transport technology.

## AI usage declaration

title: docs: correct the stale workspace-bump note and record the 0.7.0 lessons
body:
Follow-up to #223, which ran into this note being wrong.

## The correction

The workspace-bump callout said **five** crates declaring `version = "0.2"`. Both numbers were stale: **six** crates depend on `trust-tasks-rs` (`-didcomm-v1` was missing from the list), and the workspace was at `0.6` when #223 needed it.

This is the note someone reads *before* attempting a leading-component bump — being stale is the one thing it can't afford. It now names the count, points the reader at the manifests for the actual numbers rather than repeating them here, and records that it has already been stale once so nobody trusts the literals again. `trust-tasks-ceremony` is called out as *not* in the dependent set, which is the other thing that isn't obvious from the name.

## Three things #223 established that weren't written down

**A break in `trust-tasks-rs` is usually a break in `@openvtc/trust-tasks` too.** The change that made `StandardCode` non-exhaustive also widened a TypeScript union and broke exhaustive switches there, so both libraries moved to 0.7.0 together. The existing note only ever discussed the Rust side.

**`StandardCode` is `#[non_exhaustive]` as of 0.7.0**, so adding a standard error code is no longer breaking for downstream `match` expressions — but it still requires a new `trust-task-error` spec version, because the code enum lives in that payload schema and a document carrying a code the declared version doesn't list will not validate. That coupling is easy to miss and cost real time in #223.

**`trust-task-error` is in the codegen's `SKIP_SLUGS`** and is hand-modelled in `error.rs`, so regenerating will *not* pick a new code up for you. Both SDKs also need pointing at the new version explicitly — `trust_task_error_type_uri()` and `TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI` are named in the note so the next person doesn't have to go find them.

Docs only; no code, spec, or schema touched.

title: docs(contributing): document the Authorization section convention
body:
Completes the #218 → #220 → #221 sequence.

## Why

§7.3 item 15 requires a consequential spec to describe its authorization evidence. #220 and #221 established `## Authorization` (placed after `## Conformance`) as where that goes, and eight specs now carry one — but nothing told the *next* spec author to write it.

**Item 15 has no enforcement.** Unlike `parties`, `proofRequirement`, `bearer` and the side-effect and exposure classes, it is satisfied in prose with no front-matter field: no build check, no codegen constant, no CI job. It is caught in review or not at all. That is the whole reason this needs writing down, and it's called out in all three places a contributor will look.

## What the guidance leads with

The defect every audited spec had in some form: describing the **check** — "the consumer verifies the proof, then executes" — rather than the **entitlement**. That is §7.2 item 10's confusion arriving one layer up, in prose rather than in an implementation, and it explains the audit's central finding: item 15 was substantively satisfied nearly everywhere and formally satisfied nowhere, because specs named their authority in per-spec domain vocabulary scattered through `Conformance` and `Security & Privacy` with no conventional home.

Also covered:

- **Who's bound** — consequential (`sideEffects.level` mutating/destructive, or `discloses: secret`, or `actsAsSubject: true`, or an absent declaration) *and* targeting framework 0.4+. Roughly 3 specs in 5 are consequential; 181 of 302 today.
- **Pre-0.4 specs** may carry the section anyway, marked anticipatory, so it isn't mistaken for a conformance claim.
- **"No authorization evidence" is a required answer**, not an omission — with `push/register/0.2` as the worked example of writing it well.
- **Descriptive, not prescriptive**, with item 13's bar on consent/approval declarations restated.
- **A verified assertion may itself be the authorization** (the `task-consent` design) only where the spec declares that role for a named purpose.

## Worked examples

One per shape, so an author can find the nearest match rather than start cold:

| Spec | Shape |
|---|---|
| `witness/session/submit/0.1` | Two-part evidence; why a foreign submission is `challengeMismatch`, not `presentationInvalid` |
| `vrc/relationships/issue/0.1` | Authority from a prior accepted exchange; two proofs, neither is the authorization |
| `auth/refresh/0.1` | Bearer possession as the entire authority |
| `push/register/0.2` | The no-evidence case |

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — passes, 302 specs unchanged.
- All 7 file links and both in-page anchors verified to resolve.
- Docs only: no spec, schema, or generated code touched.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance, from the registry audit that produced #220 and #221. Declared for symmetry with #205.

title: docs(specs): declare authorization evidence for the 0.4-targeting witness and vrc tasks
body:
Follow-up to #218, which added SPEC.md §7.3 item 15.

## Scope — why only three specs

Item 15 requires a **consequential** Trust Task specification to describe the class of authorization evidence a consumer needs. It is a framework **0.4** requirement, and a specification conforms to the framework version it declares in `targetFrameworkVersion`.

Of 302 specs, 181 are consequential — but only **12 target framework 0.4**, and item 15 binds only those. Of the 12: 5 are not consequential, 4 already satisfy it (`provision/integration/0.3`, `vault/upsert/0.3`, `vtc/relationships/publish/0.2`, `vtc/relationships/request/0.2` — each names an authority-bearing role *and* carries an authorization-gate error code), and **3 did not**. Those 3 are this PR.

The remaining 169 consequential specs target framework 0.1/0.2/0.3 and are **not** non-conforming. A separate PR adds the declaration to four of them on hygiene grounds, marked as anticipatory.

## What each declares

None of these specs was doing the wrong thing — each already performed the right check. The gap was that the check was stated as a step in a validation pipeline rather than identified as *the authority the task rests on*, which is precisely the confusion §7.2 item 10 now forecloses.

| Spec | Authorization evidence |
|---|---|
| `witness/session/0.1` | Membership of the exchange the session claims to witness — the session's `issuer` is one of the DIDs named in `parties` |
| `witness/session/submit/0.1` | Session ownership, plus binding to the challenge issued into that session |
| `vrc/relationships/issue/0.1` | The accepted proposal — an unsolicited delivery carries no authority however well it verifies |

`witness/session/submit/0.1` is the highest-risk profile in the registry (`mutating` + `discloses: secret` + `actsAsSubject: true`), and its declaration records something the spec previously left implicit: why a foreign submission is reported as `challengeMismatch` rather than `presentationInvalid`. The presentation may be perfectly well-formed; the defect is one of entitlement, not construction.

Each declaration is **descriptive** per item 15 — it states the evidence the task assumes, states that the decision remains the consumer's own, and declares nothing about consent or approval (item 13's bar). No new normative gates are introduced.

## Two review points

**A new `## Authorization` section convention.** No spec had one; the content was scattered through `Conformance` and `Security & Privacy`, in per-spec domain vocabulary. Placed after `## Conformance`. This is the part most worth agreeing or rejecting now, before it spreads.

**No new versions, deliberately.** §5.2's draft errata rule: an editorial change to a `draft` artifact — explicitly including "rewording descriptions and other prose" — **MUST** be made in place within the existing version and **MUST NOT** mint a new one, because doing so "inflates the registry, grows the generated libraries, and forces implementations to straddle wire-identical versions for no behavioural gain." These are prose-only with no wire change.

## Validation

title: ci: assert that generated bindings agree with the specs they came from
body:
Three defects have now shipped through a green board — the response-type drop (#174), the `Payload` alias (#215), and two transport bindings merged, published and invisible on the registry site (#216). They are not unrelated:

> **The drift checks compare each generator's output to *itself*.** An output that is consistently wrong is consistently clean. And the hand-maintained lists were compared to nothing at all until someone happened to look.

This closes the first half — a check that asks whether the generated binding agrees with the **specification it came from**.

## What it asserts

`scripts/check-bindings-conformance.mjs`, run by a new **`bindings match specs`** job, for all **302** published spec versions:

- a generated module exists in each language and declares the expected `TYPE_URI`
- `$defs.Response` present ⟺ the module exports a response type and URI — **in both directions**, so §4.4.1's `MUST NOT` for fire-and-forget specs is enforced rather than assumed
- an object-rooted schema's `Payload` alias resolves to an interface or object type, not a hoisted `$ref`
- `SPEC` / `RESPONSE_SPEC` and the Rust trait consts match the front matter, including **§7.3 item 5's party swap** on the response variant
- no generated module claims a Type URI no specification declares

## Verified against the defects it exists for

A check that cannot fail is worse than none, so each was reintroduced into a generated module and the failure confirmed:

| Simulated | Result |
|---|---|
| #215 — `Payload` aliased to a hoisted scalar | ``TypeScript exports `Payload = Ext9`, but this schema's root is an object and Ext9 is a bare alias`` |
| #174 — response half dropped | ``$defs.Response declared, but the TypeScript module exports no RESPONSE_TYPE_URI and no Response type`` |
| A policy constant disagreeing with its spec | ``TypeScript request isProofRequired is false, but spec.md front matter says true`` |

## Two things worth being precise about

Overselling a check is how the next one gets skipped, so:

**It adds nothing for staleness.** A front-matter change with no regeneration *already* fails drift — I confirmed that rather than assuming it. What this adds is the case drift structurally cannot see: **the generator itself being wrong**, where regenerating faithfully reproduces the wrong output and every diff is empty.

**The comparison is three-way** — front matter, Rust, TypeScript. The two generators share no code, so a slip in either surfaces as disagreement with the other, independent of whether this file's reading of §7.3 is right. Relatedly, `expectedPolicy()` **deliberately re-implements** the derivation instead of importing the generator's helper. Sharing it would assert only that the generator agrees with itself — the property that already held while both defects shipped. That is said in the header, because the instinct to DRY it up will be strong and acting on it would hollow the check out.

## Also in here

- **PR workflows no longer filter on `branches: [main]`.** A stacked PR ran *none* of these jobs and reported a green board made entirely of DCO and licence checks. That is how #215's board read as passing when nothing had actually run — worse than reporting nothing.
- **`spec_const_emission.rs` no longer claims to cover "every spec in `specs/`".** It covers six, by hand, of three hundred. A test that misstates its own coverage is precisely what stops the real check being written. Kept as a fast Rust-side canary, with a docstring that now says so and points at the real check.
- **CLAUDE.md** gains a table of what each check does and does not assert.

## Not in here

The remaining gap from the same family: nothing verifies the **deployed** site serves what §6.2 requires — Type URIs resolving under `Accept: application/schema+json`, unknown URIs returning a real 404. `test:infra` exercises the CloudFront function in isolation, not the thing users hit. That was the shape of the defect #173 turned up, where the framework's one mandatory consumer check had never been satisfiable from the published registry. Worth a post-deploy smoke job, as its own change.

Refs #173.

title: feat(framework): make duplicate-execution protection normative (§7.2 item 11)
body:
Closes #202.

## The gap

Every piece was already present — globally unique `id`s (§4.3), audience binding (§4.8.2), a retry defined as the bit-for-bit identical document (§8.4), and an idempotency cache recommended in §10.1 — but that last one was a **SHOULD in a section marked non-normative**. So two conforming consumers could both validate a repeated document correctly, and one of them execute the transfer, the deletion, or the key rotation a second time. The framework had strong document-identifier uniqueness and no execution uniqueness to match it.

§7.2 item 11 closes that, keyed on the document `id` and scoped to *consequential Trust Tasks* (the term #218 added, which is why this issue got cheaper to land). The rule is deliberately **blind to intent**: at the document layer a hostile replay and a legitimate transport retry are the same bytes arriving twice, and what matters for interop is that the second arrival doesn't repeat the effect.

## The four things #202's suggested text didn't answer

I flagged these when reviewing the issue; they're what the extra prose is for.

1. **Retention was unbounded.** "Once a consumer has accepted a document with a given `id`" implies remembering forever. Fixed by making the retention window and the execution window *the same window*: a consumer must retain the record for as long as it will still execute the document, and no longer — a document it would now refuse as stale can't be replayed into a second execution. `expiresAt` fixes both when present; the consumer's own freshness bound over `issuedAt` fixes both when it isn't. A consumer that can establish neither has no window and **MUST NOT** execute a consequential task at all.

2. **`id` alone can't do the job.** Rejecting id-reuse-with-different-content requires storing a **digest**, not an `id` — an `id` alone cannot distinguish the retry it must absorb from the conflict it must reject. Sameness is RFC 8785 canonical equality, which is the identity §8.4 already uses for a retry.

3. **It read as contradicting §8.4.** §8.4 tells producers to retry bit-for-bit; item 11 tells consumers not to re-execute. That's complementary, not contradictory, but only if both say so — §8.4 now carries the other half: retry is safe *because* item 11 absorbs the duplicate, and a producer that re-signs or re-stamps `issuedAt` has not retried, it has issued a different document under a reused `id`.

4. **Fire-and-forget had nowhere to go.** "Return the previously determined result" assumes a success response exists; §7.3 item 7.6 explicitly contemplates tasks with none. Now stated: there is nothing to return, the consumer declines to execute, and the silence is correct rather than an error. A duplicate is never `taskFailed` — the task didn't fail, it already happened.

Also: §12.1 gains the **RFC 8785** reference, which §4.11 has been citing as `[[RFC8785]]` without it being listed. Pre-existing, fixed here because this PR cites it too.

## `idConflict` — the expensive part

You chose to mint the code rather than overload `malformedRequest`. Recording the full cost, since it's the bulk of the diff:

| Change | Why forced |
|---|---|
| `trust-task-error/0.4` | `idConflict` is absent from `0.3`'s enum **and** doesn't match its extended-code pattern, so a document carrying it wouldn't validate as `0.3` |
| Both SDKs emit `0.4` | Same reason. Per §5.2 forward-minor, a `0.3` consumer SHOULD accept it |
| `StandardCode` → `#[non_exhaustive]` | Breaking in itself, taken deliberately and once — otherwise *every* future standard code forces a major bump on every consumer. This is the last time |
| `trust-tasks-rs` 0.6.5 → **0.7.0** + six pinned crates | The §5.2 workspace event, in `publish.yml`'s dependency order |
| `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.6.5 → **0.7.0** | The widened `StandardCode` union breaks exhaustive switches the same way |
| `trust-tasks-https` → 409 | `idConflict` is a conflict. Its status table also gained a wildcard arm sending future unmapped codes to **500**, so a framework revision no longer fails to compile here — a server-side failure to keep up is not a client error |

**CLAUDE.md and the CHANGELOG are both stale on this**, which is worth knowing before the next bump: they say five crates pinned at `version = "0.2"`. Reality is **six** at `0.6`. I corrected the CHANGELOG note (and recorded that `trust-tasks-ceremony` isn't in the set, since it doesn't depend on `trust-tasks-rs`); CLAUDE.md is left alone as it's outside this change's scope.

## Verification

- `cargo build` / `clippy -D warnings` / `fmt --check` / `test --workspace` — all clean.
- **43/43** TS runtime tests; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `npm run smoke` imports the built package (381 exports).
- `npm run validate` — 303 specs (302 + the new error version).
- `npm run check-bindings` (the #219 job) — 303 specs against 303 TS and 299 Rust modules, all agreeing.
- Both generators reproduce committed output; the only non-generated deltas are the hand-written `_runtime/codes.ts`, `_runtime/document.ts`, and `error.rs`.

The `#[non_exhaustive]` break was caught by the compiler in `trust-tasks-https`, not by inspection — worth noting as evidence the workspace bump was real rather than theoretical.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance. Declared for symmetry with the originating issue.

title: Make duplicate-execution protection normative for consequential Trust Tasks
body:
## Summary

The framework already contains the main building blocks needed to handle retries and replay safely:

- §4.3 requires producers to mint globally unique `id` values and not reuse them;
- §4.8.2 addresses cross-recipient replay through audience binding;
- §8.4 defines a retry as re-sending the **bit-for-bit identical Trust Task document**, with the same `id`, `payload`, and `proof`; and
- §10.1 explicitly recognizes same-recipient replay and recommends an idempotency cache keyed by `id`.

The remaining gap is that duplicate-execution protection is not a normative consumer requirement. §10.1 says consumers handling assertions whose effects persist between exchanges **SHOULD** maintain an idempotency cache.

For Trust Tasks with mutating, destructive, secret-disclosing, or representative effects, this appears weaker than the execution risk warrants.

A legitimate retry and a same-recipient replay may be indistinguishable at the Trust Task document layer. The important interoperability invariant is therefore not merely whether replay can occur, but that receiving the same valid task again does not unintentionally repeat a consequential effect.

## Impact of the issue identified

Two conforming consumers could safely validate the same repeated document but behave differently:

- one suppresses duplicate execution based on the Trust Task `id`;
- another executes the requested effect again.

For consequential tasks this could result in duplicate issuance, transfer, deletion, key rotation, disclosure, or repeated action on behalf of a subject.

This means the framework currently provides strong document-identifier uniqueness without providing an equally strong execution-uniqueness requirement.

The issue also becomes more important as Trust Tasks are carried over asynchronous or retry-oriented transports, where duplicate delivery can be an expected operational condition rather than necessarily an attack.

## Suggested path to resolution

Move the minimum duplicate-execution invariant into §7.2 Consumer requirements while retaining §10.1 as explanatory security guidance.

The normative rule should:

1. apply to Trust Tasks whose declared or authoritative runtime behavior is consequential;
2. use the Trust Task document `id` as the duplicate-execution key;
3. distinguish a duplicate while execution is in progress from a duplicate received after completion;
4. reject reuse of the same `id` with different document content; and
5. make clear that transport request IDs, message IDs, or execution handles are not substitutes for the Trust Task `id`.

Idempotency as a property of the underlying operation can remain task-specific. The framework-level requirement only needs to ensure that transport retry or replay does not accidentally invoke a consequential operation twice.

## Suggested normative text

Add to §7.2 Consumer requirements:

> **Duplicate execution.** A *consumer* processing a *Trust Task* whose declared or authoritative runtime characteristics include a mutating or destructive side effect, disclosure of a secret, or action on behalf of a subject **MUST** implement duplicate-execution protection keyed by the Trust Task document's `id`.
>
> Once a *consumer* has accepted a document with a given `id` for execution, receipt of the same document again **MUST NOT** cause the consequential effect to be executed a second time unless the individual *Trust Task specification* explicitly defines repeated execution as safe and intended.
>
> Where the original execution remains in progress, the *consumer* **SHOULD** return or expose the existing execution state rather than initiate another execution.
>
> Where execution has completed, the *consumer* **SHOULD** return the previously determined result or an equivalent receipt where the individual *Trust Task specification* permits this.
>
> A *consumer* receiving the same `id` associated with different document content **MUST** reject the later document and **MUST NOT** treat it as a retry of the original.
>
> Transport request identifiers, transport message identifiers, or execution handles **MUST NOT** substitute for the Trust Task document `id` for the purposes of duplicate-execution protection.

§10.1 can then refer back to this requirement while retaining the broader replay threat discussion.

## AI usage declaration

The text content of this issue was developed with the assistance of AI tools for editing and formatting. This is being declared for transparency even though the Working Group / Task Force has not published guidance requiring or prescribing disclosure of AI-tool usage in issue submissions.

title: docs(contributing): document the Authorization section convention (#222)
body:
docs(contributing): document the Authorization section convention (#222)

SPEC.md §7.3 item 15 (#218) requires a consequential Trust Task specification
to describe the class of authorization evidence a consumer needs. #220 and #221
established `## Authorization`, placed after `## Conformance`, as where that
goes — eight specs now carry one — but nothing told the next spec author to
write it.

Item 15 is satisfied in prose and has no front-matter field, so unlike
`parties`, `proofRequirement`, `bearer` and the side-effect and exposure
classes there is no build check, no codegen constant, and no CI job that
notices a missing section. It is caught in review or not at all, which is
exactly why it needs to be written down. Noted in the TL;DR, in the section
itself, and as a review obligation under Submitting a PR.

The guidance leads with the defect every audited spec had in some form:
describing the *check* ("verify the proof, then execute") rather than the
*entitlement*. That is §7.2 item 10's confusion arriving one layer up, in the
prose rather than in an implementation, and it is why the audit found the
requirement substantively satisfied nearly everywhere and formally satisfied
nowhere — specs named their authority in domain vocabulary, scattered through
Conformance and Security & Privacy, with no conventional home.

Also covers: which specs are bound (consequential, targeting framework 0.4 or
later, with the fail-safe reading of an absent declaration); how to mark the
section as anticipatory on a pre-0.4 spec; that stating "no authorization
evidence" is a legitimate and required answer; that the declaration is
descriptive and item 13's bar on consent and approval declarations applies
unchanged; and that a verified assertion may itself be the authorization only
where the spec declares that role for a named purpose.

Four worked examples, one per shape: two-part evidence, authority from a prior
exchange, bearer possession, and the no-evidence case.

title: docs(specs): state authorization evidence for four pre-0.4 consequential tasks
body:
Companion to #220. Both follow from #218 (SPEC.md §7.3 item 15).

## These are not conformance fixes

Item 15 binds specifications targeting framework **0.4**. These target 0.1 and 0.2, so **none of them is non-conforming** — each declaration is marked in the spec as *anticipating* the requirement rather than claiming conformance to it. #220 carries the three specs item 15 actually binds.

They're here because an audit of all 302 specs found item 15 substantively satisfied almost everywhere and formally satisfied nowhere: specs describe the authority they rest on in per-spec domain vocabulary, scattered through `Conformance` and `Security & Privacy`, with no conventional location. These four described it nowhere at all, and in each case the authority is worth stating on its own merits.

## What each declares

**`auth/refresh/0.1`** — the clearest gap in the registry. Authorization is **possession of the `refreshToken` and nothing else**. The spec already called the token "bearer material" under a confidentiality heading without ever identifying it as *the authority*. Stating it explains two things the spec previously left unconnected: why `proof` is optional here and its absence explicitly not an error, and why rotation is the recommended theft-detection mechanism — with no second factor in the authorization, replay of the consumed token is the only signal available.

**`auth/passkey/enroll/finish/0.1` and `/0.2`** — the enrollment record named by `enrollmentId`, plus the subject bound at ceremony start. Records that the WebAuthn attestation verification establishes the *authenticator* is genuine, which is a property of the credential and not an entitlement to enroll it against this subject.

**`chat/message/0.1`** — being the expected author for the conversation and `direction`. Records that the `prev` chain check is an integrity property, not an authorization input: a correctly chained message from an unexpected author is still unauthorized, and the two failures are reported separately.

**`push/register/0.2`** — **no authorization evidence at all**, which is exactly the case item 15 says should be stated explicitly rather than inferred from silence. That's safe only because a freshly-registered handle is inert: empty allowlist, wakes nobody. The `controllerVtaDid` carried here is evidence for a *later* `push/provision` — asserted by the party that benefits from it, and checked in the exchange where it applies, not this one.

## Deliberately not touched

`push/register/0.1` was in the audit's gap list but is **`retired`**, and §5.3 freezes prose at retirement. It is left alone; `0.2` is its live successor.

## Same conventions as #220

- `## Authorization` section placed after `## Conformance`.
- Descriptive per item 15 — no new normative gates, nothing about consent or approval (item 13's bar).
- **In place, no new versions**, per §5.2's draft errata rule for wire-identical prose changes.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — passes, 302 specs (unchanged count confirms no version minted).
- Generators reproduce committed output byte-for-byte; no library regeneration or version bump.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance from a read of each spec's existing conformance rules. Declared for symmetry with #205.

body:
docs(specs): declare authorization evidence for the 0.4-targeting witness and vrc tasks (#220)

SPEC.md §7.3 item 15, added in #218, requires a consequential Trust Task
specification to describe the class of authorization evidence a consumer needs
in order to interpret the task correctly. The requirement binds specifications
that target framework 0.4; of the twelve that do, three are consequential and
did not carry the declaration.

Each already performed the right check — the gap was that the check was stated
as a step in a validation pipeline rather than identified as the authority the
task rests on, which is exactly the confusion §7.2 item 10 now forecloses:

* witness/session — membership of the exchange the session claims to witness,
  verified by matching the session's issuer against the DIDs named in `parties`.
* witness/session/submit — session ownership plus binding to the challenge
  issued into that session. This records why a foreign submission is reported
  as `challengeMismatch` and not `presentationInvalid`: the presentation may be
  perfectly well-formed, and the defect is one of entitlement.
* vrc/relationships/issue — the accepted proposal. An unsolicited delivery
  carries no authority however well it verifies, and neither of the two proofs
  on this exchange is the authorization.

Each declaration is descriptive per item 15: it states the evidence the task
assumes, states that the consumer's decision remains its own, and declares
nothing about consent or approval (item 13's bar).

Prose only, in place, no new versions: §5.2's draft errata rule requires an
editorial change to a draft artifact to be made within the existing version and
forbids minting one for a wire-identical change. `cargo run -p
trust-tasks-codegen`, `cargo fmt --all` and `npm run build-ts-bindings`
reproduce the committed output byte-for-byte, so no library regeneration or
version bump is required.

Introduces `## Authorization` as the conventional home for the item 15
declaration, placed after `## Conformance`. No spec had one; the content was

hoisted-alias `Payload`, and a policy constant that disagrees with its spec.

Two things worth being precise about, because overselling a check is how the
next one gets skipped:

The comparison is three-way — front matter, Rust, TypeScript. The two
generators share no code, so a slip in either surfaces as disagreement with the
other, independent of whether this file's own reading of §7.3 is right. And
`expectedPolicy()` deliberately re-implements the derivation instead of
importing the generator's helper; sharing it would assert only that the
generator agrees with itself, which is the property that already held while both
defects shipped. Said so in the header, because the instinct to DRY it up will
be strong and acting on it would hollow the check out.

It adds nothing for staleness. A front-matter change with no regeneration
already fails drift. What it adds is the case drift structurally cannot see: the
generator itself being wrong.

Also:

- **PR workflows no longer filter on `branches: [main]`.** A stacked PR ran none
  of these jobs and reported a green board made entirely of DCO and licence
  checks — which is how #215's board read as passing when nothing had run.
- **`spec_const_emission.rs` no longer claims to cover "every spec in
  `specs/`".** It covers six, by hand, of three hundred. A test that misstates
  its own coverage is what stops the real check being written; the docstring now
  says what it is (a fast Rust-side canary) and points at the real one.
- CLAUDE.md gains a table of what each check does and does not assert.

Refs #173.

title: docs(infra): bring the CloudFront README up to date with what is deployed
body:
The function now negotiates two subtrees; the README described one. Written while running the deployment in #198, so every note here is something that actually bit or that I had to check.

## The one that would have caused damage

The **"Updating the function" example hard-coded the old `Comment`**. `update-function` replaces the whole config rather than patching it, so following the README verbatim would have silently reverted the comment to a stale description. Both the create and update examples are corrected, with a note that `--function-config` uses `key=value` shorthand and therefore **splits on commas inside the comment** — which fails with `Invalid type for parameter FunctionConfig.Comment … type: <class list>`, an error that does not obviously point at the comment. That one cost me a round trip.

## New guidance, all of it earned

**Diff the LIVE function before publishing.** The distribution is not managed from this repository, so the deployed function can differ from `main`. I checked with `get-function` + `diff` before publishing and it was byte-identical — but had it not been, I would have shipped someone elses undeployed change alongside mine without noticing.

**Test in the real runtime, not just Node.** `npm run test:infra` exercises routing under Node; CloudFront runs a constrained ES5.1 engine, so a green suite does not prove the function works where it runs. `test-function` executes the DEVELOPMENT stage against a synthetic event, and the window between `update-function` and `publish-function` is exactly when to use it.

**⚠️ The rewrite target must exist before the function goes live** — a new ordering rule that mirrors the existing SPA-error-mapping one and points the *opposite* way. There the function must lead; here it must follow, because a negotiation rule points at an object on the origin. So: deploy the website first, then publish the function.

With a corollary worth its own line: **verify the object with `aws s3 ls`, not through CloudFront.** Until `ASSET_PREFIXES` knows about a tree, CloudFront serves the SPA shell for it and tells you nothing about whether the object exists. During the deployment `/ceremonies/…/ceremony.json` returned `200 text/html`, which looks like success and means the opposite.

## Corrections

- Title and intro cover both subtrees, and say why ceremony definitions negotiate on `application/json` rather than `application/schema+json` — a definition is an *instance* of the ceremony format, not a JSON Schema.
- The routing table gains the ceremony rewrite and `/ceremonies/`, plus why the disjointness of `/spec/` and `/ceremony/` (SPEC §6.7) has to be held by **prefix** tests: singular and plural share a long common prefix, so a substring test would match both and loop.
- A second ⚠️ beside the `ROOT_FILES` one — `ASSET_PREFIXES` must track the published trees, since a tree synced into `website/` but unlisted is swallowed by the SPA fallback.

## verify.sh

The README now claims `verify.sh` covers ceremonies, so it does — five new checks: the definition as JSON, the page for a browser, the raw asset, an unknown definition 404ing honestly, and a Type URI asked for as plain JSON **not** resolving into the ceremony tree.

**13 checks, all passing against the live site.** The CloudFront unit suite is still 21/21.

title: feat(ceremony): support the offline bilateral shape, and stop over-fitting to VTC
body:
Committee feedback against an offline two-person protocol found three rules that only hold when a maintainer is present. Each is fine for the shape the note was tested against — **that is the finding**.

Every flow in the corpus is **mediated**: VTC onboarding, `task-consent`, `credential-exchange` all have a maintainer or community always present and always online. Three properties of that *sample* were written down as properties of *ceremonies*.

The uncomfortable part: ADR 0001 chose "ceremony" for its security-literature sense — a protocol extended to include **human participants**, as in a key-signing ceremony. Two people meeting in person is the most ceremony-shaped interaction there is, and it was the one shape the design could not express.

## Demonstrated, not asserted

Running a mutual-attestation definition through the publication checker:

```
mutual prev          -> "prev graph has a cycle" + "nothing can open the enactment"
two prev-less steps  -> "2 required steps have empty prev; deadline origin ambiguous"
```

Inexpressible, not merely awkward.

## The three fixes

**`coDerived` anchor (§7.3).** `prev` does two jobs — causal dependency, and the origin the enactment is measured from. A simultaneous exchange has the second without the first. A definition now declares its anchor: `openingStep` (default, every mediated flow) or `coDerived`, where the anchor is the enactment identifier itself, jointly derived by the roles in `boundBy` from something neither party could produce alone. Since `ceremony.enactment` is signed, every step signing it *is* every step committing to the shared anchor. An anchor bound by one role is rejected — that is an opening step wearing a disguise.

**Bilateral `countersigned` (§7.5–7.6).** "Far too heavy as a default" is true of a twelve-step mediated flow and backwards for two people, who are present and signing anyway. It was also listed as needing a definition because "the participant set must be known"; in a bilateral ceremony it is evident from the documents — so such an enactment verifies with **no definition**, which is what makes it work with no network *at verification time*, not merely at enactment time.

**Issuance-window `maxDuration` (§9).** The draft rejected a step "arriving after the deadline", conflating a **stale command** with a **settled record**. A ceremony that completed inside its window stays complete however long its documents took to travel — and offline, they travel late by design. `now` never enters the comparison.

The companion rule requiring a steps `expiresAt` to fall inside the deadline is **dropped, not repaired**: it defended against replay into a closed enactment, which signing `ceremony.enactment` already prevents outright. A rule duplicating a stronger guarantee only creates ways to be wrong.

## Layering (§2.3), from the second feedback batch

> A ceremony **MUST NOT** mandate what is verified or created by its steps.

A definition names Type URIs; what those tasks carry — DTG credentials, acknowledgements, nothing — belongs to those specifications. Two ceremonies producing entirely different artifacts, or none, are the same kind of object. The corollary matters more than the rule: **a ceremonys evidence and an artifacts validity are separate questions.** A design that let a ceremony vouch for credentials minted inside it would have made every ceremony a certificate authority.

## Referencing a ceremony from outside it (§10.1)

§4.9.1 (name an exchange by its initiating document `id`) and §4.11.2 (name a flow by its `enactment`) are **different scopes**. A context field bound to `threadId` can express *"came out of that task"* and cannot express *"came out of that ceremony"*.

Three consequences an external specification must decide for itself: completion evidence is not artifact validity; **participation is not authority** (§4.11.4 and §7.2 item 9 already say so for the envelope member); and an enactment identifier embedded in a durable artifact is a worse correlation handle than in a step, because a credential may be shown for years to anyone — cite a commitment the holder can open selectively.

## Enforcement and evidence

- `anchor` in the definition format; `maxDuration` redocumented as an issuance window
- Checker: opener rule respects anchor kind, `countersigned` + recorders rejected, bilateral countersigned reported as verifiable from step documents alone
- **`ceremonies/mutual-attestation/0.1`** — a real definition of the offline shape, validating, built only from Type URIs the registry serves
- Fixtures **14 → 18**, with per-case `base` so anchor rules test the shape they govern, and each base asserted to pass before its mutations are trusted

One fixture failed on first run and was right to: my "every step follows another under a coDerived anchor" check was **unreachable** — such a graph is either a cycle or names a missing step, both already caught — and the fixture asserted a legitimate ordered pair was invalid. Check and fixture both removed.

§16 gains a fourth round, and it is the only one that needed someone outside the corpus.

title: fix(ts-bindings): identify a schema's root type by title, not by position
body:
> Stacked on #214 — base retargets to `main` automatically when that merges. The diff here is this change alone.

Found while regenerating for #214. **`Payload` aliases the wrong type in the TypeScript bindings for 14 published specifications.**

`rootTypeName()` took the first `export interface|type` in the compiled output, on the assumption that the root always comes first. It does not: where a schema `$ref`s a shared definition, json-schema-to-typescript may hoist that definition to its own exported type *ahead of* the root, and the first-match rule picked it up. So `chat/message/0.1`, `trust-ceremony-receipt/0.1`, `consent/request/1.0`, both `audit/*`, all three `task-consent/*` — and `vrc/relationships/issue/0.1` and `witness/session/submit/0.1`, published yesterday in #213 — each exported:

```ts
export type Payload = DigestMultibase;   // = string
```

in place of their request payload interface.

## Why nothing caught it

Worth stating, because the same gap will hide the next one:

- **The drift check compares the generator's output to itself.** A consistently wrong alias is consistently wrong, so drift is clean.
- **`tsc --noEmit` is satisfied** — the alias is well-formed TypeScript.
- **No test asserts what `Payload` resolves to.**

Same failure mode as the response-type drop fixed in #174, and it survived for the same reason: the rule that had to be right was a positional guess about compiler output.

## The fix

The root is identified by the name the compiler derives from the schema's own `title` — the same derivation json-schema-to-typescript uses — and only where that name is actually present in the emitted output. Position remains the fallback for a schema carrying no usable title.

A positional guess replaced by a better guess is still a guess, so this carries **an invariant**: an object-rooted schema whose root resolves to a *bare* alias (`= string`, `= DigestMultibase`) now fails the build, because that is the shape this failure always takes.

Scoped to bare aliases deliberately. An earlier draft rejected any `export type` root and took out `auth/revoke-session`, `credential-exchange/issue` and `keys/import`, which legitimately compile to `export type X = { … }` — an object type literal, and a union, are both valid root forms. The narrowed check leaves those alone.

## Versioning

**Not treated as a breaking change**, despite changing compile-visible types on 14 specs. The old alias was unusable: assigning a real payload to a `string` does not compile, so no correct consumer could have depended on it — the only code that compiled against it was code passing a string, which meant nothing. Bumped **0.6.3 → 0.6.4**.

The Rust bindings were never affected (`pub struct Payload` is generated from a different path). `trust-tasks-rs` 0.6.4 is unchanged in content and moves only to keep the two libraries in step, per CLAUDE.md's convention — no dependent-crate version requirements move.

## Verification

`npm run build-ts-bindings` emits **349 modules, none dropped**; **zero** bare-alias `Payload` exports remain, down from 14. `npm run validate` green at 298 specs, `tsc --noEmit` clean, TS suite 43/43, `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt` green, and `git diff trust-tasks-rs/src` is empty.

Refs #173. Stacked on #214.

title: feat(specs): converge the remaining bare-hex digests onto DigestMultibase
body:
Finishes the sweep #214 began. Two bare lowercase-hex SHA-256 members were left in the registry, both scoped out there because their blast radius was larger and their defect narrower:

| Spec | Member | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `vault/_shared` | `VaultEntry.attachments[].sha256` | `digestMultibase` |
| `provision/integration` | `summary.digest` | `digestMultibase` |

**No bare-hex digest now remains in any current specification version.**

## The defect, and what it is *not*

Both hard-coded one algorithm into the wire contract — moving off SHA-256 would need a schema revision rather than a different multihash prefix — and named no base encoding, leaving a verifier to infer base16 from context.

Unlike the credential digests in #214, both are taken over **opaque bytes** rather than a JSON document, so **no canonicalization defect is being fixed here**. #214's third and worst problem — three specs promising the same value with no way to guarantee it — does not apply. This is the encoding argument alone, and each new description now states what its digest is computed over so the distinction stays on the record rather than being re-litigated.

Where it does bite: under `provision/integration`'s **`pinnedOnly`** assertion mode this digest is the holder's *sole* integrity anchor for the sealed bundle. An anchor whose algorithm is fixed by the schema cannot be strengthened without breaking every holder that already pinned one.

## Why this PR has the shape it does

The vault change arrives through a **shared component**, and [§5.4](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#54-migrating-between-versions)'s coupling rule says a specification cannot adopt a new shared component version without issuing a new version of itself. So `vault/_shared/0.3` carries the converged `AttachmentRef`, and the three specs that expose `VaultEntry` — and therefore its attachment digests — bump with it: **`vault/get/0.3`, `vault/list/0.3`, `vault/upsert/0.3`**.

**`vault/proxy-login` and `vault/release` deliberately stay on `_shared/0.2`.** They reference only `SiteTarget` and `SecretKind`, never reach an attachment digest, and §5.4 explicitly permits a specification to remain pinned to the older component rather than bump for a change it does not carry. Bumping them would have been churn dressed as thoroughness.

## Deliberately not converged

**`AndroidApp.sha256CertFingerprints`**, in the very same shared file. Its colon-separated uppercase hex is Google's format — emitted by `apksigner` and the Play Console, and matched against an app's actual signing certificate. That is an **externally-owned value**, carried verbatim per [SPEC §4.10](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#410-naming-conventions). Converting it would break the only thing it exists to compare against. Flagging it explicitly so a later sweep doesn't "finish the job".

## Versioning

Breaking on the wire, released as `MINOR` increments under [§5.2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#52-compatibility-rules)'s `draft` allowance. Every superseded version stays published, pinned and generated, so this is **additive to the libraries** — `0.6.4 → 0.6.5`.

`provision/integration/0.3` also drops `0.2`'s `wireCompatibleWith: "0.1"`, which no longer holds: `0.3` is wire-identical to neither. All four specs move to `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"`.

Each new version carries a **Changes from 0.2** section with the reasoning and the §5.4 migration sequence.

## Verification

`npm run validate` green at **302 specs / 60 shared schemas**; both drift checks clean; `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo test --features validate`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt`, `tsc --noEmit` and the TS suite (43/43) green. Confirmed the superseded versions are byte-identical (`git diff` on `_shared/0.2`, `get/0.2`, `integration/0.2` is empty), and that #215's root-type fix holds on the new modules — `Payload` aliases to the real interface on all four.

Refs #173. Follows #214.

title: feat(framework): separate authorization from identity and proof validation (§7.2 item 10)
body:
Closes #205.

## What

Generalizes the identity/proof-versus-authorization boundary from the two narrow places the framework already states it to every Trust Task, and names the class of task the stricter rules apply to.

- **§2** — defines *consequential Trust Task* as `sideEffects.level ∈ {mutating, destructive} ∨ exposure.discloses = secret ∨ exposure.actsAsSubject = true`, with the fail-safe reading of an absent or unresolvable declaration folded in.
- **§7.2 item 10** — a consumer **MUST NOT** treat successful validation of a VID, `issuer`, `recipient`, transport-derived identity, or `proof` as establishing that anyone is authorized to request or perform the task, and **MUST** evaluate authorization separately before executing.
- **§7.3 item 15** — a consequential specification **MUST** describe the class of authorization evidence it presupposes, under the same descriptive-not-prescriptive discipline as items 13 and 14.
- **§4.11.4 and §7.2 item 9** — retargeted at item 10 so the ceremony rule reads as an instance of the general rule rather than a competing statement.
- **Appendix B** — 0.4 changelog entries.

## Why

The principle is already in the spec twice: ceremony membership grants nothing (§4.11.4, §7.2 item 9), and the side-effect and exposure classes describe a task without authorizing it (§7.3 items 13–14). It was never stated for an ordinary Trust Task, which leaves an implementer free to read

> valid `proof` + recognized `issuer` + correct `recipient` = authorized instruction

That is the confused-deputy vector §4.11.4 forecloses, reached by a different route. It matters most where the producer is an autonomous agent: such a producer can prove its own identity perfectly while holding no authority to act for a subject, exercise a delegated capability, disclose information, or cause a consequential effect.

## Design decisions worth reviewing

**The rule is model-neutral.** It requires that an authorization decision be *made*, not how. The framework prescribes no delegation, consent, capability or governance model, and item 10 does not constrain which evidence a consumer consults.

**The `task-consent` carve-out is preserved explicitly.** A verified assertion may still *be* the authorization — that is the whole point of `task-consent/decision/0.1`, where the proof on the decision, not the session that carried it, is the authorization. Item 10 permits this only where the specification defines that role *and* the consumer's policy accepts it, so it is a deliberate design a spec adopts, not a default a consumer may infer. §7.3 item 15 gives it a declaration site.

**§7.2 item 10 is appended, not inserted.** SPEC.md, the bindings and the specs collectively reference §7.2 items 5, 7 and 9 by number; appending leaves every existing reference correct.

**§7.3 item 15 is a prose declaration with no front-matter field.** The issue's suggested text could be read as adding a machine-checked declaration. I deliberately did not: that would mean a `spec.meta.schema.json` change, a build-validation change, and re-auditing ~30 spec families before CI goes green. Item 15 says so explicitly so nobody adds the field by accident. If we do want it machine-checked, that should be its own PR.

## Scope / follow-ups

- **§7.3 item 15 is a new MUST on consequential specifications**, and existing specs have not been audited against it. Most already describe their expected authority in prose, but that has not been verified spec-by-spec. Worth a follow-up issue rather than blocking this one.
- The remaining four issues in this batch (#202, #203, #204, #206) all depend on the `consequential` definition landed here; #204 in particular depends on item 10 for the "who may cancel" question.
- SPEC.md's header still reads **Document version 0.3** while Appendix B has an open 0.4 section. Pre-existing, not touched here.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — passes; 302 specs validated, 410 example documents checked. The three `vta/did-templates` warnings and the one unparsed fenced block are pre-existing and unrelated.
- All internal anchors added by this change resolve.
- §7.3's ordered list confirmed contiguous 1–15 through the indented continuation paragraphs.

**No regeneration or version bump.** This is prose-only: no payload schema, no framework schema, no front-matter field changes. Nothing in `trust-tasks-rs` or `@openvtc/trust-tasks` is generated from it, and no generated constant (`IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` and friends) moves.

## AI usage declaration

Drafted with AI assistance, on a human-reviewed reading of the current SPEC.md and of #205. Declared for symmetry with the disclosure on the originating issue.

title: Generalize the identity/proof-versus-authorization boundary across all Trust Tasks
body:
## Summary

The current framework already contains an important authorization boundary for Trust Ceremonies.

§4.11.4 states that ceremony membership is a claim rather than a permission, and §7.2 item 9 says a consumer **MUST NOT** grant authority on the basis of ceremony membership alone. It further states that authorization decisions rest on `issuer`, `proof`, and the consumer's own policy.

§7.3 also makes clear that side-effect and exposure declarations are descriptive and do not themselves authorize execution.

These are useful safeguards.

The remaining ambiguity is that the framework does not state the identity/proof-versus-authorization boundary equally explicitly for an ordinary Trust Task request outside ceremony membership.

Successful verification of an `issuer`, VID, transport-derived identity, or document `proof` establishes important facts about identity and document integrity. Those facts do not necessarily establish that the producer is authorized to request the described outcome or that the consumer is authorized to execute it.

At the same time, the repository's `task-consent` work demonstrates an important nuance: a verified proof **can** constitute authorization evidence where an individual Trust Task specification and the consumer's policy explicitly give the signed assertion that meaning.

The framework would benefit from making this distinction general.

## Impact of the issue identified

Without a general statement, an implementer could infer:

> valid proof + recognized issuer + correct recipient = authorized instruction.

That inference is particularly risky for agentic and delegated execution.

An agent may be able to prove its own identity while lacking authority to:

- act for a subject;
- exercise a delegated capability;
- disclose information;
- mutate protected state; or
- cause a destructive action.

The current ceremony-specific language substantially reduces this risk inside ceremonies, but the same principle should apply consistently to all Trust Tasks.

## Suggested path to resolution

Generalize the authorization-separation principle already present in §4.11.4 and §7.2 item 9.

The framework should remain authorization-policy neutral. It need not prescribe a particular delegation, consent, capability, or governance model.

The required invariant is narrower:

> identity and proof validation are evidence inputs; they do not automatically establish execution authority unless the applicable task specification and consumer policy explicitly define the verified assertion as authorization evidence.

Individual consequential Trust Task specifications should describe the class of authority expected where that is necessary for interoperability, while leaving the final authorization decision to the consumer and applicable governance framework.

## Suggested normative text

Add to §7.2 Consumer requirements:

> **Authorization is distinct from identity and document-proof validation.** Successful validation of a VID, `issuer`, `recipient`, transport-derived identity, or document `proof` **MUST NOT**, by itself, be interpreted as establishing that the *producer* is authorized to request the outcome described by the *Trust Task* or that the *consumer* is authorized to perform it.
>
> A verified assertion **MAY** constitute authorization evidence where the applicable *Trust Task specification* explicitly defines that semantic role and the *consumer*'s policy accepts the assertion for that purpose.
>
> Before executing a *Trust Task*, a *consumer* **MUST** evaluate any authorization requirements applicable under the individual *Trust Task specification*, the consumer's own policy, and the applicable trust or governance framework.
>
> Such evaluation **MAY** include delegation, mandate, capability, membership, standing, credential status, subject relationship, purpose limitation, or other authorization evidence.
>
> Failure of authorization after successful document validation **SHOULD** be reported as `permissionDenied` where an error response can be returned safely.

Add to §7.3 Specification requirements:

> A specification whose successful execution can cause a consequential side effect, disclose a secret, or act on behalf of a subject **MUST** describe any class of authorization evidence that is necessary to interpret the task correctly. Such a declaration **MUST NOT** be interpreted as requiring a consumer to authorize execution merely because the described evidence is present.

## AI usage declaration

The text content of this issue was developed with the assistance of AI tools for editing and formatting. This is being declared for transparency even though the Working Group / Task Force has not published guidance requiring or prescribing disclosure of AI-tool usage in issue submissions.

§7.3 gains item 15, requiring a consequential specification to describe the
class of authorization evidence it presupposes, under the same
descriptive-not-prescriptive discipline as items 13 and 14. It is satisfied
in prose and has no front-matter field, so spec.meta.schema.json and the
build are untouched.

§2 gains *consequential Trust Task*, naming the predicate
sideEffects.level in {mutating, destructive} or exposure.discloses = secret
or exposure.actsAsSubject = true once instead of re-spelling it at each use,
with the fail-safe reading of an absent declaration folded in.

Additive: the wire format is unchanged, every document conforming to 0.3
still conforms, and no payload or framework schema changes, so the
generated libraries need no regeneration or version bump.

Refs #205

title: feat(specs): converge the remaining bare-hex digests onto DigestMultibase (#217)
body:
feat(specs): converge the remaining bare-hex digests onto DigestMultibase (#217)

Finishes the sweep #214 began. Two bare lowercase-hex SHA-256 members were left
in the registry, both flagged as out of scope there because their blast radius
was larger and their defect narrower:

  vault/_shared        VaultEntry.attachments[].sha256   -> digestMultibase
  provision/integration  summary.digest                  -> digestMultibase

Both hard-coded one algorithm into the wire contract — moving off SHA-256 would
need a schema revision rather than a different multihash prefix — and named no
base encoding, leaving a verifier to infer base16 from context. Unlike the
credential digests in #214, both are taken over opaque BYTES rather than a JSON
document, so no canonicalization defect is being fixed here; this is the
encoding argument alone, and each new description says what its digest is
computed over so the distinction is on the record.

It matters most under provision's `pinnedOnly` assertion mode, where the digest
is the holder's SOLE integrity anchor for the sealed bundle. An anchor whose
algorithm is fixed by the schema cannot be strengthened without breaking every
holder that already pinned one.

The vault change arrives through a shared component, which decides the shape of
this PR. `vault/_shared/0.3` carries the converged AttachmentRef, and per SPEC
§5.4's coupling rule a specification cannot adopt a new shared component version
without issuing a new version of itself — so the three specs that expose
`VaultEntry`, and therefore its attachment digests, bump with it:

  vault/get/0.3, vault/list/0.3, vault/upsert/0.3

`vault/proxy-login` and `vault/release` deliberately stay on `_shared/0.2`. They
reference only `SiteTarget` and `SecretKind`, never reach an attachment digest,
and §5.4 explicitly permits a specification to remain pinned to the older
component rather than bump for a change it does not carry. Bumping them would
have been churn dressed as thoroughness.

Deliberately NOT converged: `AndroidApp.sha256CertFingerprints` in the same
shared file. Its colon-separated uppercase hex is Google's format, emitted by
apksigner and the Play Console and matched against an app's actual signature —
an externally-owned value, carried verbatim per SPEC §4.10. Converting it would
break the only thing it exists to compare against.

`provision/integration/0.3` also drops `0.2`'s `wireCompatibleWith: "0.1"`,
which no longer holds: `0.3` is wire-identical to neither.

Breaking on the wire, released as MINOR increments under SPEC §5.2's `draft`
allowance; every superseded version remains published, pinned and generated, so
this is additive to the libraries. All four specs move to
targetFrameworkVersion 0.4. Bindings regenerated (302 specs, 60 shared schemas,
both drift checks clean); libraries bumped 0.6.4 -> 0.6.5.

No bare-hex digest now remains in any current specification version.

Refs #173. Follows #214.

title: feat(bindings): didcomm-v1/0.2 — move the carriage to a dedicated message type
body:
`bindings/didcomm-v1/0.1` §2 shipped with a ⚠ open flag on its carrier: it rode an Aries `basic-message` for **reach**, and asked whether that was the right call at all. @albertoleon7794 answered it properly — built the identical exchange **both ways** against Credo 0.6.3, measured, and retired the reach argument themselves ([`ref-06v1d-carrier`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06v1d-carrier)). This settles it as a specification change, which is what we owed them on #173.

## The carrier moves; the attachment does not

| | `0.1` | `0.2` |
|---|---|---|
| `@type` | `basic-message` (two interchangeable URIs) | `https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm-v1/0.2/trust-task/1.0/task` |
| Document slot | `~attach`, `@id` `trust-task` | **unchanged** |
| Human-readable line | `content` (RFC 0095) | optional advisory `comment` |

**Why the dedicated type wins**, per their measurement and recorded in §2.1:

- **It is *less* code in Credo** — ~25 lines — once `basic-message`'s content-only high-level API and its attachment-dropping message store are priced in. `0.1`'s own §2.2 documented both as costs; they were the reason.
- **It crosses a mediator identically.** v1 forwarding is type-agnostic — the type is inside the envelope.
- **It leaves the chat store alone.** `basic-message` writes every Trust Task into a wallet's conversation history, a real user-facing surface.
- **A consumer needs a handler under every option**, so reach only ever bought *visibility*, never function.

What `basic-message` genuinely retained is **visible degradation in a mixed fleet** — an unaware wallet shows a harmless "Trust Task: …" line where a dedicated type is dropped silently. §2.1 records that as an accepted loss rather than arguing it away: capability negotiation ([SPEC §11](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#11-discovery-and-capability-negotiation), RFC 0031) is what gates a peer speaking Trust Tasks, so a peer that never negotiated should not be sent one.

The attachment arguments were about the *slot*, not the carrier, so they carry over intact.

## Also in 0.2

- **The `@type` is an [RFC 0020](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/concepts/0020-message-types) message type URI**, and §1 gives its decomposition so Aries tooling routes it as a protocol rather than an opaque string. Minted at `0.2` and **pinned** across later MINORs, exactly as `binding/didcomm/0.2` keeps `binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope`.
- **`0.1`'s two-interchangeable-URIs hazard is gone**, not restated — our own type has one spelling. It survives only inside §2.3, where a consumer still meets `basic-message`.
- **§2.3 requires a `0.2` consumer to accept the `0.1` carriage**, and forbids a `0.2` producer from emitting it — §5.4's receivers-first sequence. A `basic-message` carrying *no* `trust-task` attachment is explicitly **not** a Trust Task and must not be answered as one.
- **Targets framework `0.4`**, clearing the bump #208 flagged as out of scope.

## On calling this a MINOR

`0.1`'s §6 said a carriage change is breaking and requires a `MAJOR`, and in general it is right. §6.1 argues the number rather than asserting it — three reasons it is honest here:

1. **A `0.2` consumer accepts everything a `0.1` producer emits** (§2.3). That is the direction [§5.2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#52-compatibility-rules) makes normative, satisfied in full.
2. **`0.1` anticipated this** — its §6 closed by saying a pre-adoption carriage change should be a correction to the draft rather than a new major. A new MINOR is the *more* conservative reading: it gives implementers a distinguishable URI instead of changing `0.1` under anyone who already built against it, and `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` 0.1.0 is published, so somebody could have.
3. **§5.2 permits it explicitly** while an artifact is `draft`.

And what is **not** preserved is stated plainly rather than implied: **forward compatibility**. A `0.1` consumer does not recognise a `0.2` message and drops it silently. No versioning scheme fixes that across a carriage change; deployments migrate receivers first and negotiate capability before sending.

## A registry gap found while doing this

`window.TT_BINDINGS` in `website/assets/bindings.js` is hand-edited, and `npm run build` only *copies* the bindings tree — it never enumerates it. So **`didcomm/0.2` and `didcomm-v1/0.1` were both merged, published, implemented, and completely invisible on the registry site**, for as long as nobody looked.

Same hand-maintained-list failure as the category taxonomy, so it gets the same treatment: all three missing entries added, plus **`checkBindingRegistry()`**, which fails the build on an on-disk binding with no entry or a `prosePath` that does not match its `id`, and warns on a listed binding with no directory. Verified it actually fires by removing an entry and confirming the build fails — a guard that cannot fail is worse than none. Documented in CLAUDE.md alongside the existing `data.js` callout.

No library changes: this touches no `specs/`, so no bindings regenerate and no version bumps. `npm run validate` green at 298 specs, `npm run build` clean.

## @albertoleon7794 — two things

**The `@type` value is the piece most worth your review.** I used an RFC 0020-conformant form so Credo's `parseMessageType` decomposes it into protocol `trust-task` / version `1.0` / message `task`, rather than mirroring the v2.1 binding's flat `…/envelope` URI. You have the Aries deployment experience; if Credo's routing or discover-features prefers a different shape, say so and it changes — nothing depends on it yet, which is precisely the window we spent too much of already.

**`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` still implements the `0.1` carriage** and needs updating for this version, alongside the `thid` omit-rule from #208 you offered to send. Happy for both to come from you as one PR, or we can take it — whichever you prefer.

Refs #173.
